REQUEST FOR FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO SNOWBOUND AREAS OF SOUTHWESTERN ONTARIO-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity pursuant to the provisions of Standing Order 43.
In view of the disastrous snowstorm which struck southern Ontario this past weekend isolating hundreds of small communities and bringing normal daily life to a standstill; in view of the fact that much of this region has been declared a disaster area and that many municipalities are still on an emergency alert basis; in view of the fact that a second storm appears to be on its way and that many roads are still impassable; and considering that most municipal budgets, particularly those in the Niagara Peninsula, are heavily overspent, that costs so far have already run about twice that of a normal year and that storms such as that of last weekend are costing a single municipality about $6,000 to $7,000 per hour to clear, and while thankful for the excellent relief assistance already provided by the local militia, I would like to move, seconded by the hon. member for Welland (Mr. Railton):
That this House urges the federal government to consult immediately with the responsible provincial and municipal officials with a view to providing necessary disaster relief whether through financial means or physical assistance and that it give consideration to absorbing or defraying the cost of relief provided by the militia and the Department of National Defence.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jack Cullen (Minister of Manpower and Immigration) moved
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
that Bill C-27, to establish the department of employment and immigration, the Canada employment and immigration commission and the Canada employment and immigration advisory council, to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, and to amend certain other statutes in consequence thereof, be read the second time and referred to the standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I intend to concentrate my remarks today on the two main objectives of Bill C-27, the employment and immigration reorganization act, and to outline the basic reasons underlying the changes proposed in the bill. The tirst objective is to bring about the integration of the Department of Manpower and Immigration and the Unemployment Insurance Commission. The second is to introduce certain changes into the unemployment insurance program.
On the subject of integration, Mr. Speaker, the main question I have had in my mind as the new minister of this complex portfolio is why integration is now appropriate, bearing in mind the decision taken about ten years ago to separate the employment service from the Unemployment Insurance Commission. A central factor is that conditions in the Canadian society-economy and the labour market of the late 1970s- are significantly different than they were in the late 1960s.

During the last decade there has also been an important evolution in our manpower programs and in unemployment insurance. Manpower services generally, and in particular the counselling, placement, training and mobility programs, as well as the newer job-creation programs, have greatly strengthened and matured. At the same time, the unemployment insurance program has been extended to cover almost the entire labour force and has come to play a much more significant role in the operation of the Canadian labour market and the Canadian economy. Indeed, we now have some of the most advanced employment and insurance programs in the world.
As a result of these changes, Mr. Speaker, the destinies of the Department of Manpower and Immigration and the Unemployment Insurance Commission have become ever more closely linked. Indeed, the complementary nature of the work of the two organizations is illustrated by the fact that half of the claimants for unemployment insurance benefits now register with Canada manpower centres. Such claimants constitute 70 per cent of the total clientele of CMCs.
As a result of these developments, the two organizations have come to co-operate more and more closely, and ways have been developed to harmonize their programs and activities. This has been reflected, for example, in increased efforts to expose UI claimants to the counselling and job placement facilities of CMCs. While this harmonization and co-operation have yielded significant and positive results, it has become clear that a unified management is required to provide the best services to the Canadian public.
Specifically, we believe that integration will lead to substantial improvements to services through, first, a rationalization of the present network of local offices of the Unemployment Insurance Commission and the Department of Manpower and Immigration; second, the conversion of most service points into one-stop centres where the complete range of services of the two organizations would be available to the public; third, the faster and more systematic exposure of clientele to employment services; and lastly, a simplification of the documentation required of clients and a streamlining of the procedures to be followed by them in using the services provided under the employment and insurance program.
It is also important to bear in mind, Mr. Speaker, that the immigration program has had, and will continue to have, a far-reaching impact on the Canadian labour market. Thus, the inclusion of immigration in the mandate of the new organization will be essential to the achievement of an integrated approach to the development of employment programs. I say this recognizing, of course, the important social objectives and consequences of our immigration program.
The new integrated organization will consist of both a commission and a small support department. The new Canadian employment and immigration commission will be responsible for the administration of labour market programs and the policies underlying those programs. These will include the payment of benefits under the unemployment insurance program, immigration, recruitment, selection, settlement, enforce-
February 1, 1977

ment and control, placement, counselling and training, and the administration of other employment programs such as direct job-creation. It will also provide the administrative support functions for both the commission and the department. The support department of employment and immigration will be responsible for strategic policy development, program evaluation, labour market research and information services. It will help to ensure the closest possible linkages between labour market policies and program and the government's over-all economic and social strategies.
The effective fulfillment of the mandate of the commission will continue to require close co-operation and consultation between government, labour and business. Thus, the well-established policy of tripartite consultation and co-operation will be continued through the representation of workers and employers in the new commission. Indeed, the potential for effective co-operation will be enhanced, since the authority of the new commission will extend not only to the unemployment insurance program but also to labour market programs generally as well as immigration matters.
In this connection, Bill C-27 also makes provision for the establishment of a new Canada employment and immigration advisory council. Personally, I attach the highest importance to the role to be played by the new advisory council in terms of the government's approach to co-operation with the private sector in general and labour and management in particular. That is why I intend to recommend that high-level representatives of labour and management be appointed to the council, people with full authority to speak in the name of those whom they represent. In addition, there are many individuals in the community who are not directly representative of labour or management and who have significant contributions to make to the discussions on issues related to the Canadian labour market. They will also be given an opportunity to participate in the work of the council.
I should like to turn now to the second main purpose of Bill C-27, which is to introduce certain changes to the unemployment insurance program. There are three major changes proposed: first, an increase in the number of weeks required to qualify for UI benefits, so-called entrance requirement, from eight weeks to twelve; second, a change in the benefit structure which is the framework used to determine the duration of a claimant's entitlement to benefit; third, the authorization of more productive or developmental uses of unemployment insurance funds, including the use of such funds as income maintenance for claimant's participating in approved training courses, job-creation projects and work-sharing programs.
The eight-week entrance requirement to our unemployment insurance program has certainly been one of its more contentious issues on which there has been extensive discussion. For example, I have received briefs and letters strongly recommending that the requirement be increased to as many as 20 weeks. I have received equally strong recommendations that there should be no change. Those who have argued for an
Employment and Immigration
increase in the entrance requirement have done so mainly on the basis of concern about the incentive to work. An examination of the characteristics and behaviour of claimants with eight to eleven weeks of insured employment-the so-called "eight to eleven weekers"-strongly suggests that an increase in the entrance requirement would constitute for many of them an incentive to work longer. In general, eight to eleven weekers are younger than average, without dependants, and many are secondary earners in families. Basically, they have what might best be described as an intermittent or unstable attachment to the active work force.
The current entrance requirement, which is one of the most generous of any country in the world, provides an all too readily available financial inducement reinforcing unstable work patterns. In light of these characteristics and behaviour of eight to eleven weekers, it is not unreasonable to expect that a substantial proportion of them will work an additional one to four weeks required to qualify for the new twelve-week entrance requirement. For those who do not, we consider that there are other programs which are preferable alternatives to meeting their needs. These are the kinds of programs I announced in the employment strategy, ranging from the rehabilitative measures of training to actual employment in job-creation projects.
Another question which has been asked is: Why choose 12 weeks rather than, say, 15 or 20 weeks?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext: Or 30.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Our investigations have indicated that the eight to eleven weekers receive a significantly higher degree of subsidization from the unemployment insurance account and have a much more unstable attachment to the labour force than any other category of insured worker. In light of these factors, our judgment is that the twelve-week entrance requirement is, on balance, the most appropriate.
The second proposed change is the introduction of a new benefit structure. This will have several advantages. It will be simpler than current arrangements. It will be based on three phases, two of which are related to the number of weeks of insured employment and the third of which is related to local unemployment conditions. This will facilitate an easier comprehension of benefit entitlement and will simplify administration of the act. The new arrangements for benefit entitlement will also be more equitable. In particular, there will be a better balance between the number of insured weeks that a claimant has, and the number of weeks of benefit to which he is entitled in the initial phase of his claim. Provision will continue to be made for additional benefits for those with a longer labour force attachment. Finally, entitlement to regionally extended benefits will be much more sensitive to local unemployment conditions because it will be based directly on regional unemployment rates.
Thus, the new benefit structure is designed to curtail benefit entitlement to those with a relatively short labour force attachment living in regions of low unemployment. At the same time, it is designed to maintain appropriate insurance protection to

Employment and Immigration
those with longer labour force attachment as well as to those claimants who reside in regions of high unemployment.
Other changes will also be introduced into the benefit structure to enhance the motivation for work. For example, we propose to eliminate the four-week rule which now results in a claim being terminated if a claimant returns to work for four weeks in the extended benefit phase. This rule has proved to be a disincentive for claimants to return to employment, particularly when there is some uncertainty about the duration of that employment.
The changes in the entrance requirement and the benefit structure must be considered in the context of our over-all employment strategy. The savings arising out of these changes in the UI program will be redirected to programs designed to create new employment opportunities as well as to help prevent unemployment. In this way we will achieve a more effective allocation of resources in support of a range of employment programs tailored to meet the needs of those individuals, groups and areas of the country most seriously affected by unemployment.
There are a number of other specific amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act which are proposed. For example, the right to appeal decisions of boards of referees will be broadened to give all claimants and employers the right to request an appeal to the umpire against the unanimous decision of the board of referees. At present, only claimants and employers represented by associations can appeal such decisions as a right. This amendment will be implemented after changes have been introduced in the appeal system in light of the findings and recommendations of the Law Reform Commission. I should also explain that Bill C-27 makes provision for an increase in the number of Federal Court justices who can hear appeal cases, in order to reduce the number of outstanding appeals.
The final area of proposed change in the unemployment insurance program is the introduction of authority to use unemployment insurance benefits in more directly productive or developmental ways. In this connection I should stress that unemployment insurance will continue to provide a vital measure of income protection to unemployed workers while they conduct an active job search to locate the most suitable and satisfying employment available to them. In this way the program plays a very productive role in Canadian society in maintaining skills, preserving dignity and preventing economic hardship.
There are instances, however, when the productive impact of the program is inhibited by factors such as obsolete or inappropriate skills, or the absence or shortage of employment opportunities in a particular area. In these circumstances the role of the UI program to facilitate job searches has, inevitably, a diminished applicability. I believe, therefore, that there is a need to work out program alternatives that would permit a more productive use of time while on claim. To this end I am proposing three developmental uses of unemployment insurance funds, two of which would be launched on a limited pilot basis.

First, the developmental use of unemployment insurance funds would provide for a streamlining of income maintenance arrangements for claimants on manpower training courses. We know that many individuals are unemployed because they lack appropriate skills, and that many of these individuals can benefit from occupational training or retraining. Under this proposal, trainees eligible for unemployment insurance on federally-sponsored training courses would normally receive their full unemployment insurance benefit as their main source of income maintenance.
This contrasts with the current arrangement under which claimant-trainees receive manpower training allowances, topped up with unemployment insurance benefits, when their level of unemployment insurance benefit entitlement is higher than their allowances. From the standpoint of developmental impact, this rationalization of financial arrangements should lead to a more effective allocation of resources and could, potentially, free-up resources for additional training.
Mr. Speaker, the second proposed developmental approach is the use of unemployment insurance funds as income maintenance for claimants on special job-creation projects. There are large numbers of unemployed workers receiving unemployment insurance benefits who cannot find employment, while at the same time many community-oriented projects cannot be carried out because of lack of funds to pay for such work. Under the proposed arrangements, unemployment insurance claimants would be given the opportunity of participating in job-creation projects on a purely voluntary, basis while they receive unemployment insurance benefits.
This approach would enchance the scope of job-creation projects and increase the number of individuals who could participate in them. I am very much aware that this is a new area which would require careful experimentation and evaluation. We would, therefore, propose to launch it on a pilot project basis to assess its proposed impact on unemployment and the labour market.
The third proposed developmental use of unemployment insurance funds would be in work-sharing arrangements. At present, when a firm faces a temporary emergency it normally cuts back on production and reduces the size of its work force. Many of the workers who are laid off will search for other work, move, seek training for a new occupation or remain unemployed. Typically, there are major losses involved in this process. Workers' skills may erode when they are idle and some of them may lose the habits and patterns of work that are important to their personal and economic well-being. When the firm is ready to rehire, it may find some of its former work force with weakened skills and some no longer available.
Work-sharing could reduce these problems. For instance, instead of one-quarter of a work force in a particular establishment being laid off, employers and workers could agree that it would be preferable for all of the work force to work a 30-hour week instead of a 40-hour week on a temporary basis. During the period of the arrangement, unemployment insurance ben-
February 1, 1977

efits would be paid for one-quarter of a week to all of the workers instead of for all the week to one-quarter of the workers. We also propose to launch this program on a pilot project basis to permit a careful evaluation of its results and potential impact and to ensure the support of workers and employers.
Mr. Speaker, Canada has had a very favourable reputation as an innovator in the field of labour programs and policies, and I think we have, in the proposed developmental use of unemployment insurance funds, another opportunity to demonstrate that spirit of innovation. It is a spirit conditioned by a sensitivity to the practical difficulties which could be involved. This is why we would propose to proceed with the job-creation and work-sharing projects on an experimental basis. Such experimentation is not necessary in the case of training, where we have had substantial experience with the training of unemployment insurance claimants and where our proposals involve mainly a rationalization of financial arrangements.
The annual funding level for all of the developmental projects will be set by the governor in council.
These, Mr. Speaker, are the main changes proposed in Bill C-27 and a brief explanation of their underlying rationale and objectives. We will, of course, have an opportunity of examining all of the areas in greater detail during the committee stage, at which time I will be presenting additional information on the proposed changes.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, once again we are involved in what I call a very significant debate. This is the third time we have had an opportunity to become involved with a bill which in its original form was brought forward in 1971, when it certainly brought about a lot of problems. The government has been playing around with it since then, hoping that eventually they could come up with an unemployment insurance scheme that the people would accept.
Today we are debating amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act. I want to repeat what the minister has indicated as the highlights. It provides for the establishment of a department of employment and immigration, the establishment of a Canada employment and immigration commission, the establishment of an employment and immigration advisory council, and the establishment of a three-phase benefit structure. The latter is actually an overhaul and simplification of the method used to determine a claimant's entitlement to benefit; that is, the benefit structure as proposed. The existing structure, based on five benefit periods, would be replaced with a simplified three-phase structure. In other words, the minister has found out that the five-phase structure was unworkable, cumbersome and inefficient. The three-phase structure will be made up of an initial benefit period, the labour force extended phase and a regional extended phase.
The initial phase is structured on the basis of strict insurance principles which would require that the number of weeks of benefit to which a claimant is entitled is closely related to the number of weeks a claimant has worked. One week of
Employment and Immigration
benefit would be allowed, therefore, for each insurance week of employment from a minimum of 12 to a maximum of 25 weeks. This move is long overdue. In the labour force extended phase, one week of benefit would be allowed for every two insurance weeks of employment over 25 insurance weeks. A maximum of 13 weeks benefit would be payable in this phase. The regional extended phase recognizes the need of high unemployment for additional income protection. From two to 20 weeks of benefits would thus be payable in this phase, reaching the maximum when the regional unemployment rate exceeds 8.5 per cent.
It is interesting to note that the government understands there is a problem with the regional differences that are maintained through its own ineptness and its mismanagement of the economy. It has now recognized the severe economic problems faced by people, say, in the Atlantic provinces and the province of Quebec as related to other regions of the country. The minister has admitted something further. The over-all maximum entitlement under the new benefits structure would be 50 benefit weeks to be drawn within a 52-week period. There is not much change there, Mr. Speaker: it was previously 51 weeks; now it is 50.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext: That is too generous.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
It is also proposed to do away with the present four-week rule which now results in a claim being terminated if benefits are not paid during four consecutive weeks in an extended benefit period. This rule is considered a serious disincentive to claimants who might otherwise take short-term jobs. All members have had many letters pointing out the inequality of this provision. It actually prevented people from taking that further step to try to become part of the labour force.
Another matter upon which I shall dwell at some length later, and which the minister tried to justify, is the increased pension requirement from eight weeks to twelve weeks. The government stole that policy without giving us notice.

speechtext:
Back in 1971, when fewer were unemployed and the economy was healthier, I remember telling the minister who was responsible for bringing in this monstrosity of a law to include in the program incentives for work. I suggested that 12 weeks of employment should be a minimum qualifying requirement, but the minister said no. Mr. Speaker, I made that point six years ago.
It is apparent the government is not aware that national policies can effect detrimentally certain regions of the country. It is about time it began considering the realities of the new federalism. I understand that the thinking of the government has changed in that national unemployment insurance funds are to be used for training purposes. The minister elaborated on the point at some length. In other words, those on federally-

Employment and Immigration
sponsored courses are to receive full UI benefits. These, not manpower training allowances, apparently would be their main source of income. We must explore this proposal. The minister suggested that he is not sure how it will work, and that is why this will be a pilot project. The next pilot project mentioned involved job-creation. The next involved work-sharing. One can only conclude that after six years of thinking about them the government has come forward with pilot projects because it is not sure how they will work. Since they are to be pilot projects, we will need to examine them thoroughly.
There is another point which I am not sure the minister mentioned in his speech. We all heard what he said today- and he did not say a heck of a lot. I do not think he said that the right to appeal, which is now so restricted, discriminatory and harmful to claimants, will now be granted both to claimants and employers. I think such a move would be a step in the right direction because the provisions of the existing legislation are disastrous.
I understand that the National Employment Service Commission is to continue to function; it will continue to collect information, to ensure that discriminatory acts do not take place, and it will define and obtain information for the use of the commission. The minister neglected to say-not deliberately, I think-that the experience rating provision introduced by the former minister has now been judged to be disastrous. No regulations thereunder have ever been passed. I think the minister nods his head in approval of that statement. We brought the situation to the attention of the previous minister, but no, he disagreed with us-the experience rating provision was the greatest thing since sliced bread. Now, seven years later, once more the government says that the opposition was right. I do not mind taking a little credit on behalf of my party.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
I suggest that hon. members should read the speeches members of my party have made and read what has been said in committee. If they do that, they will find that it has been our position that the experience rating provision is cumbersome, discriminatory and of limited effect. We said that in 1971. How the government opposite has survived in power is beyond me. It has stayed in power by procrastinating, playing hanky-panky with the people and giving away the taxpayers' dollars. It has not developed policies, as we showed some time ago.
I have dealt with some of the matters with which the bill deals. My colleagues in this party and other parties will explore various aspects of the bill, the introduction of which gives us all the opportunity to discuss the dismally unsatisfactory record of this government in developing the country for

the benefit of Canadians and creating jobs and growth, the potential for which could make us the envy of the free world.
When we discuss the economy of this country, we are discussing a sad state of affairs. The minister has brought in this bill in these sad times. As the Conference Board of Canada, the University of Toronto Institute of Policy Analysis, and the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development have made clear, in 1977 and 1978 we shall face high unemployment, slow growth and some continuation of inflation. Those respected organizations have painted a picture of doom and depression facing this country, a situation which warrants a statement by the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau) with regard to the state of our economy so that the people of Canada may know what prospects they face. Unfortunately, the statements of those respected organizations, and our demands for a statement to show the people the kind of mess we are in, have fallen on deaf ears. The respected organizations mentioned have indicated that we shall have more jobless in this country unless Ottawa acts swiftly.
Mr. Speaker, many figures have been bandied about, but it is accepted generally, I think, that in 1978 about 875,000 of our people will be unemployed. In short, we must stimulate new business activity and increase consumer spending. Surely, the gloomy picture which has been painted is a powerful argument for the introduction of a budget, the highest priority of which ought to be job-creation. I say this because at present some 780,000 people, making up about 7.5 per cent of the labour force of Canada, are unemployed.
Unfortunately, the government has merely paid lip service to the solution of the unemployment problem. At present, the unemployment rate in Newfoundland is about 13.6 per cent; in New Brunswick, 11.1 per cent; in Prince Edward Island, 9 per cent plus; and in Nova Scotia, 9 per cent plus. We have learned lately of the unsatisfactory employment picture in Quebec where unemployment is running at about 10 per cent. The indications are that conditions will get still tougher in this country.
For all these reasons it is clear that the government has no idea of the extent of this country's unemployment or how to correct it. Surely, therefore, we ought to address ourselves to providing further business investment tax credits, cutting personal income taxes for those in low and middle income groups and bringing about the early removal of controls in order to restore the confidence of the business community and encourage needed investment.
When the government introduced its control program, it stole the idea from us. Unfortunately, it did not steal the right policy, which is why we are in our present mess. The government should have been wise enough to impose the freeze we advocated: it ought to have introduced a consultative process involving labour, management, concerned groups and provincial governments prior to the imposition of controls. In that way we could have known in which direction we ought to go. But the government did not do that. Instead, it chose to bring in its own version of that policy, with the result that the entire country is exercised about it.
February 1, 1977

speechtext:
I hear hon. friends to my left. With that sort of calibre, is it any wonder that they cannot get any more than 15 or 16 seats. Milton Friedman stated:
We know how to do it. Every economist knows how to do it. I can specify it very simply. The only way to cure inflation is for the government to spend less and to print less. The only way to cure inflation is to hold down the growth in the quantity of money. There is no other way to do it. There is no device which will allow us to slow down inflation. The problem, however, is not how to stop inflation. The problem is to have the political will to do so.
In other words, Milton Friedman was talking about having the guts to move in the direction of stopping printing money and spending money. It has to stop. Failing that, we will end up as some other countries the names of which I will not mention for the moment. What concerns me is that this government does not have the intestinal fortitude to proceed accordingly and to give top priority to the problem of unemployment. The only thing it can think about now is bringing in amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act, and we do not know whether they will be effective or not. The human cost of the neglect of this government, in terms of job-creation, is staggering. We pay about $4 billion in unemployment insurance between the government and the employer-employee premium. We lose billions of dollars in lost productivity, and we lose taxes in the millions, goodness knows how much, just as the result of this government not having as its top priority the creation of jobs.
That is the climate in which this government introduces amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act, woefully ignoring the fact that tinkering now and again with the act is not the answer. The answer is the creation of jobs, if you want to reduce large expenditures on unemployment and reduce, if not eliminate, abuses and suspicions about unemployment insurance.
Employment and Immigration
With regard to this act, I had the opportunity to obtain advice from some of the provincial governments throughout this country. I would like to place on record a precis of some of the concerns that have been exhibited. One, the social assistance payments to the provinces may go up due to the eight to twelve-week change. Another, that the provinces be compensated for the loss of moneys from the UI payment by the use of funds for manpower training and job creation. Next, that genuine and close consultation occur between the provinces and the federal government prior to the implementation of the manpower program so that provincial priority needs will be met and the funds will be allocated in a way tailored to the provinces. Another point is that inadequate time was given for the provinces to make budgetary arrangements to offset the loss of revenue from the UIC changes or the planned programs to offset their negative effects. Another point made was that co-operation, co-ordination and consultation between the provinces and the federal government appeared in almost every letter as a key concern.
Let me talk about the province of Saskatchewan. Saskatchewan, as I understand it, is committed to the use of direct employment programs in an attempt to meet the objectives of the Saskatchewan manpower policy. Year-round job creation aimed at high unemployment areas is not one of its highest priorities, since its economy is strong. More important to them is the maintenance of current volumes of employment, should an economic downturn occur in the future, in order to avoid out-migration of labour. The new policy should co-ordinate programs in a way designed to permit individuals to gain access to permanent employment with career promotional opportunities. They do not want more fragmented, short-term federal employment schemes. They feel that the eligibility for training with UI funds should not be restricted to UI recipients. They want assurances that federal funding under manpower training programs now in existence will not be curtailed. I do not know whether the minister knows all this. I will send him the letters, if he wants to see them.
I want to get into work-sharing in some detail. I do not know whether the minister is aware of the problems in Germany and other places in that regard. Saskatchewan feels it is a good idea, that it is consistent with their provincial manpower policies, but employers and employees should be consulted to ensure that the proposal does not interfere with the collective bargaining process. The low rate of unemployment in Saskatchewan, about 3 per cent, means that workers are subsidizing the unemployed in other provinces through their unemployment insurance payments.
What about Ontario? They agree generally with the conclusion of the federal analysis of the legislation and the changes indicated that are needed. They especially agree with the recommendation that efforts are needed to remove work disincentives and unnecessary costs from the program. However, they have some concern about the heavy reliance of the proposal on unemployment insurance as a means for income redistribution. That is the policy this government has been following for some time. Rather than have an insurance

February 1, 1977
Employment and Immigration
scheme, they have used it as income redistribution. Not only is the province of Ontario concerned about that but other provinces are also.
Another point the province of Ontario raised is that major unemployment insurance costs come from persons with weak labour force attachments, that is, the eight to eleven-weekers. Evidence suggests that raising the eligibility period from eight to twelve weeks will not result in a substantial increase in welfare costs. Evidence gathered by the Unemployment Insurance Commission review indicates that many people after eight to eleven weeks of work do not need to resort to welfare for income. The review doubts that alternate compensation schemes will be necessary. On the whole, it feels changes will be advantageous to Ontario and will put government funds to more productive use.
How about New Brunswick? They indicated that Unemployment Insurance Commission benefits will be reduced by $30 million in 1977; that is, a combination of Bill C-69 and the new changes. This will increase the social assistance burden of the province. They felt there was insufficient consultation; there was not enough lead time for them to express their concerns to the degree that they would have liked; that there was not enough time given for them to prepare, provincially, their budget to accommodate the increased social assistance burden or to develop alternate programs to offset some negative implications of the changes. They too, want discussion and consultation on the employment strategy; in other words, the Young Canada Works program envisaged by the minister as job-creation and work-sharing. They want to have input into their development because it should reflect the manpower, economic and social policies of New Brunswick. They also state they must have provincial consultation during the development of the program if the program is within provincial jurisdiction. With regard to work-sharing, this province is concerned that a doubling of staff may be needed to administer it, and that co-operation exist between labour and management and both levels of government. They, too, say that savings from the UIC should return to the provinces in such a manner that positive, continuing-I repeat, positive, continuing-results occur.
What about Newfoundland, Mr. Speaker? We have ignored that province. We have shamefully neglected it, not only in regard to this aspect but in regard to all other aspects. This province has calculated that the UIC changes will cost the province $12 million to $15 million, assuming that 50 per cent of the eight to eleven-week workers find they work for the additional required weeks, as the various studies show. It has also been calculated that the federal government will spend at least that much on job-creation and manpower training programs. It is anticipated that included in the target group for new or expanded manpower programs would be welfare recipients who otherwise would have continued on unemployment insurance if the changes had not been made. The province would control escalation of welfare costs because of the changes.

As for Alberta, Mr. Speaker, they intend to support the proposed amendments because the benefit duration is more closely related to the previous labour force attachment. Alberta also states that the benefits will be more insurance-oriented than the current ones, and the over-all effect will be a minor tightening of unemployment insurance in Alberta. They also state that the federal government and the provinces together should provide income support; that therefore changes at either level can have an impact magnified by lack of deliberate consultation and co-operation between the jurisdictions. Notice, Mr. Speaker, how there is continual reference to co-operation, consultation and co-ordination. This seems to be the big thing with that province. They also state that costs added to provincial programs and services as a result of UIC changes should be compensated; that consultation take place immediately because of differences in the requirements of federal and provincial budgetary cycles.
With regard to the three-phase benefit structure, as far as Alberta is concerned they view phase 7 as the insurance phase, with benefits related to length of employment and paid from premiums. The extended phase 2 and phase 3 appear to be primarily income maintenance. Since Alberta believes that UI should be primarily an insurance scheme, phases 2 and 3 are viewed as part of the program only in the absence of a support-supplementation program.
I propose to deal now, Mr. Speaker, with some of the provisions of the act. Having brought to the attention of the minister the concerns of the provinces, I should like to talk about the integration of manpower and unemployment insurance. I have already stated that this has been our policy. We have always called for this. This is what we now call the one-step approach which was brought forth and, let us say, magnified by the Economic Council of Canada. The one-step approach envisages counselling, payment of benefits and the placement of jobs all under one roof. What we have had in the past is frustration in the area of payments, duplication of documentation, one bureaucracy paying out money and the other trying to find jobs, neither knowing what the other was doing. In my view this has cost us millions of dollars.
I have some concerns about this policy. It has not been spelled out by the minister sufficiently for us to be aware of some of the answers. What will be the function of a counsellor, as opposed to that of a benefit control officer? Will they have the same job? If so, a lot of hardship can arise, with one guy supposedly counselling a claimant and the other guy trying to kick him off unemployment insurance. We will have to watch very carefully whether they are one and the same.
Will there be greater bureaucracy as a result of this? I thought perhaps there would not be, but I have some misgivings about it now. I thought that as a result of the shifting and integrating of staff, we were talking about one group policy rather than creating a whole new bureaucracy. We will have to watch the minister in this respect, too. How long will it take, Mr. Speaker, to bring about this one-group concept? Are we close to it? I get press releases from the minister's office and his departmental officials saying that someone else has a job
February 1, 1977

and that the minister is responsible for this and that, but it does not make any sense in terms of how simple will this integration, or marriage, be so far as meeting the needs of claimants is concerned.
I have a few other points I would like to make, Mr. Speaker, with respect to the proposed new department of employment and immigration which now will have an associate deputy minister. The duties of the commission advisory council are less clearly defined. For instance, the new commission will perform duties as required in relation to any matters for which the minister is responsible. That is really a sweeping generalization, and I hope it is not true. Previously, the commission's duties related specifically to the Unemployment Insurance Act. Similarly, the advisory council will advise the minister on all matters to which the powers, duties and functions of the minister extend and is no longer assigned any particular responsibilities.
What is going on here? Is the minister not going to have anything to do? Is he going to abdicate his responsibilities? I will not tell Your Honour what I think he said; I will just continue with my speech. Nevertheless, we will want to know whether his responsibilities are staying with him, or are they going to be channelled to some nameless bureaucracy? If so, we take a dim view of that, Mr. Speaker. As I understand it, the chairman of the commission will be the deputy minister of the department; the vice-chairman will be the associate deputy minister. The chairman of the advisory council may be appointed for an indefinite term, whereas the term previously was for three years. Why this change?
Members of the advisory council may now receive remuneration as well as expenses and allowances as authorized by the governor in council. Previously, members, other than the chairman, could only receive travel and living expenses and a per diem allowance if approved by the minister-not remuneration. I would remind the minister that we are in a period of restraint, and I suggest he will have to answer for this. What is a little more disturbing is that there is no requirement that the advisory council must meet. Previously, they had to meet at least once a year.
Annual reports should be prepared by the council, and the minister should table the same in order that the public might be aware of the areas of disagreement and the consensus which exist within the membership of the council. All this has been secret so far. The minister does with it what he pleases, and we are left in the dark.
I should like to bring some other matters to the attention of the House. In the new bill there is no mention of the continued existence of the various advisory boards which are presently provided for in legislation. Where is the advisory board on adult occupation training? Where is the advisory committee on the co-ordination of rehabilitation services for disabled persons? Where is the advisory committee on the adjustment of immigrants? Where is the advisory board on manpower and
Employment and Immigration
immigration research? These are some of the questions I have to ask with respect to the merger.
Now let us turn to the 12-week amendment. The Gill report of 1962 stated that unemployment insurance should basically be a plan to deal with short-term, fractional and cyclical unemployment and that it is not an appropriate program to provide for structural unemployment or for the seasonally unemployed. In this light it recommended that a test of at least 20 full weeks of employment in the preceding year be established as the eligibility requirement, except for new entrants and those who moved in and out of the labour force frequently. The recommendations of this commission reflected the view that the minimum qualifying period should be long enough to establish that insured employment had an important, if not a principal, place in the claimant's manner of earning a living, and enough to establish that he has not entered insured employment solely for the purpose of qualifying for benefit. The objective of greater regional equalization should be met by other than an insurance scheme.
Nevertheless, eight years later the white paper on unemployment insurance, upon which the 1971 unemployment insurance amendments were based, noted that under the scheme envisaged benefits would be paid more on the basis of need than length of time in the work force, and the program in some respects calls upon the good will and responsibility of more fortunate, better placed Canadians toward those who, through lack of education and opportunity, are in less secure occupations.
Criticism came from left, right and centre-from all quarters of the country-with respect to the program brought forward in 1971. People were concerned about the work disincentives implicit in generous benefits. They were concerned about the increased importance of the welfare aspect rather than the insurance objective of the program. They were worried because they felt it was not actuarially sound.
Now, in 1977, the government is tightening up the program in an attempt to bring unemployment insurance more into line with the realistic principles of an insurance program and with the realities of the labour market by extending the qualifying period of eight weeks to twelve weeks. Coupled with the new three-phase benefit structure proposed, the twelve-week amendment will increase the correlation between real labour force attachment and access to protection through the unemployment insurance program. But Canada still enjoys, and will continue to enjoy, the most generous unemployment insurance benefits in the world. Sometimes I wonder if that is a proper position for us.
I am very much aware of the findings of studies regarding the minor employment group. I am aware that 80 per cent have no dependants; that approximately 50 per cent are under the age of 25; that many are secondary workers, working wives and youths living at home who belong to families with incomes in the middle to upper income range. There is a great tendency for these people to exhaust their benefits. Seventy per cent of all eight to eleven weekers find work within six weeks of exhausting their benefits.

February 1, 1977
Employment and Immigration
I am also very much concerned about the attitude of some provinces with respect to the possible enlargement of their welfare rolls as a result of the amendments we are considering. I am also conscious of the fact that to be unemployed in Ontario, Alberta and Saskatchewan is very different from being unemployed in the Atlantic provinces, since it is much easier to find a job in the former areas than in the latter. Economically developed areas offer greater opportunities to get jobs. In the Atlantic provinces, or the economically depressed areas of the country, opportunities are significantly less. The existence of regional disparity in all its forms calls for flexibility in our approach to this amendment.
Notwithstanding the fact that we accept the 12 weeks, what we seem to have forgotten is that in this day and age, in the new federation, national policies must sooner or later reflect the needs of the several regions of the country. That is what federal-provincial confrontation is all about. The provinces want a new federalism. They want a sensitive government, one which is aware of and concerned about their needs. As I said a moment ago, the existence of regional disparity calls for flexibility, especially at this time, in relation to the amendment before us.
We do not know how successful Canada Works will be. We do not know how successful Young Canada Works will be. The minister said he hoped some 60,000 jobs would be created. At the moment he seems to have made a boo-boo. Right now, as I understand it, the position is this: the forms were not distributed equally throughout the nation-some had them, and others did not. The time allowed for the completion and filing of these forms is unrealistic. The date is February 4. Yet the minister tells us today he is still considering whether the program should be extended. He says some $30 million has been taken up. Has he forgotten we are talking about a $200 million program?
The minister told us two or three days ago that he is still looking at this matter. Perhaps he is looking for a miracle. Something is wrong. Industrial leaders and others fear there will not be sufficient time in which to take advantage of the program. The minister can take this as notice for action.
We do not know how successful this pilot job-creation program will be, so we cannot estimate its impact upon the UIC in terms of savings. We have no idea whether the government is prepared to make job-creation a serious priority. Questions are asked of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald). Questions are put to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen). He said he does not like to reveal his plans because the opposition will make hay in terms of the unemployment rate-I am paraphrasing what the minister told me. Mr. Speaker, I do not know how seriously that gang is treating this fundamental human problem of unemployment.
I was talking a few minutes ago about regional disparity. We can see no improvement in terms of regional economic expansion. As I understand it from my hon. friend from Egmont (Mr. MacDonald), the policy is not getting the results it should be getting in terms of job-creation. To date, we do not know whether there will be an April budget designed to

stimulate the economy. The minister likes to play games. He says "before June", or "after March", or "bientot"-the minister smiles because I use that word. I am expressing a concern which is extremely important to Canadians, particularly to the 700,000 or so who are unemployed, and this number is envisaged as likely to be around 100,000 more in the future. We do not know what is happening to the Anti-Inflation Board. All I know is that the Minister of Finance believes it is harming economic development, and that officials of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce holds the same view, as does the chairman of the AIB.
So as it stands now, because of this government's insensitive and ineffective performance we feel that regional differences must be recognized not in words but in deeds. Accordingly, because of our concern and because of the lack of response by the government, I now advise the House that my party will move an amendment to clause 17. This is in general what we intend to do. We propose the following amendment:
In high unemployment regions, the minister may, with the approval of the governor in council, make regulations
-lowering from 12 weeks down to a minimum of 8 weeks the number of weeks referred to in subsection 16(1) and 17(2)(a);
-defining high unemployment regions, delineating the boundaries thereof and determining residence and eligibility within such region;
-setting a date of termination for any such regulations-
Notwithstanding the fact that we abide by and stick to the 12-week eligibility period, we find that it is time now to consider national policies to meet regional needs. That is what federalism is all about. The present uniformity of policy has created tension and frustration within confederation.
Let me now proceed to another matter which the minister has touched upon, namely, work-sharing. I know that the minister has much expertise with respect to this innovation, but I would like to make a few comments on this matter. For many years statutory unemployment insurance or assistance schemes in France, Germany, Great Britain and Sweden have contained provisions covering payments for partial unemployment. In most countries there is a limit to the time for which partial unemployment benefits are paid.
The average French manufacturing worker now receives roughly half of the regular hourly wage as short-time compensation. Short-time payments are financed partly by the company concerned and partly by the public assistance scheme. The number of workers on short time in France rose from
19,000	in July, 1974, to more than 200,000 a year later.
In Italy, short-time benefits for workers with a permanent job in either industry or construction are paid by an employer financed fund set up originally by collective agreement and subsequently covered by legislative decrees. That is an extremely important point. The benefits now replace approximately 80 per cent of gross earnings for up to 40 hours a week. Short-time benefits in this case replace a greater proportion of earnings than do regular unemployment benefits for industrial workers. A very steep rise in the number of hours compensated followed the widespread use of short-time work in Italy. In the

first half of 1975, hours compensated increased fourfold in industry and represented 3 per cent to 4 per cent of total hours worked.
In 1975 Germany increased the maximum duration of shorttime benefits from six to twelve months, and to twenty-four months under certain conditions. The scheme is primarily financed through the unemployment insurance system. Shorttime payments have played an important role in protecting many workers threatened by dismissal. The number of workers on short-time rose from 292,000 in 1974 to more than 900,000 in May, 1975. In October, more than 700,000 workers were still on short-time work schedules. The practice of work-sharing in these countries has helped to keep unemployment rates lower. However, in the three countries mentioned above the numbers of workers that were on short time went up tremendously after the institution of work-sharing, meaning the cost of unemployment insurance could have been higher than if lay-offs were used.
Is work-sharing an artificial means of lowering the unemployment rate? For example, does it mask the true magnitude of the problem? The minister will have to ask his officials to answer that question in order that we get to the truth of the matter. I am not saying the minister has misled us, but we put the minister on notice that there are significant problems with respect to this work-sharing program. If there is a question of prolonged periods of work-sharing, would some of these workers be better off retrained in a skill in demand?
The major social value to this is that the employees do not lose contact with the work world and are not completely idle. That is of major social value to the employees. According to the Department of Manpower and Immigration, their worksharing proposals will be designed to help employers retain a full force on a reduced work week, rather than laying off part of their work force. Employees who would otherwise be laid off will receive wage supplements so that their income will be higher than possible UIC benefits, but lower than their normal earnings. This will allow the employee to retain employment and save his or her possible turnover costs such as training new employees or finding new employees. Work-sharing should be implemented on a pilot project basis starting October, 1977.
There are some areas to which we should give further thought. From their description, work-sharing may not be applicable to service industries or continuous process operations. Work-sharing in these areas is better implemented through rotation of employment rather than reduction in the work day, since in industries certain hours must be kept for customer service. Let me spell out some of the advantages of this plan for work-sharing that will accrue to the employer. First, overhead costs may be lowered because of reduced operation of the plant, and so on. Second, work-related costs will fall since for all workers on work-sharing the employer will not have to make UIC contributions. Third, it will save the employer possible turnover costs when production resumes at a normal level.
However, there are disadvantages for the employee, and I want to put these on the record because it is upon these
Employment and Immigration
concerns and the answers we get that we will be able to determine whether the type of program the minister envisages will be of maximum benefit to the employee. Much union opposition stems from internal politics-the senior members generally outnumber the junior members-so that in lay-offs based upon seniority they will not be laid off. Why should they sacrifice their full salaries? Second, it may not give them enough useful time to take another part-time job or to make an effective job search. However, they have the advantage of not being completely unemployed and are receiving incomes higher than possible UIC benefits. Third, theoretically, worksharing can be a substitute for lay-offs, regardless of the extent. However, too large a reduction may result in increased UIC costs or in an income for the worker equal to UIC benefits. There must be some limit set out regarding the use of work-sharing: in some countries, and in some collective agreements, reductions beyond one-third of the work week are considered better dealt with by more appropriate methods.
Beyond a certain level, work-sharing may not be practical for the employer or tolerable for the employee, particularly for extended periods. There may be the possibility of abuse by employers wishing to take advantages of the benefits of worksharing, even though the program is to be governed by stringent eligibility criteria. One provincial premier has claimed that work-sharing will cost a tremendous amount administratively, as much as double the present cost. We will have to look into that. But the key is flexibility in designing and administering work-sharing so that it can best accommodate the needs of the employer and employee in each case.
I notice that under the bill the governor in council may make regulations. We will have to be advised of the regulations from time to time when this pilot project is brought in, so that we are aware of the problems and of the progress which we hope will be made if the program is acceptable. This may present problems in terms of the extent of the commission's power to impose an agreement on management and labour; that is, it could interfere in the collective bargaining process. The International Union of Electrical Workers has stated that although it is not against work-sharing per se, it is against government-mandated work-sharing. There may be difficulties in enforcing the program. I know, from having discussed this matter with both labour and management, that they oppose work-sharing based in part on a study of the problems encountered in other countries.
Those are my few remarks at this time. Other hon. members on this side of the House will be involved in this debate. In terms of job creation, we now throw the ball back to the minister, because if the things about which I have talked in terms of Young Canada Works, Canada Works, budgets, job-creation, the Anti-Inflation Board, and regional economic expansion programs, do not take place, then what I have done is indicate to the minister that the amendment we will be proposing shows that there is a need for us to be very much concerned about and aware of the problems caused by federal policies across this country.

So, subject to the several reservations I have mentioned, we will support the bill at second reading in order to get it into committee where many questions can be asked and answers given, hopefully to make this bill a much better one than it is at present.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is fairly obvious that there is quite a coalition here this afternoon. It is fine for the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) to talk about

unemployment, cheaters and people unemployed for a period of between eight and twelve weeks. I suspect that the unemployment rate in Hamilton is very low indeed; it is an area of high employment. I have been with the hon. member in committee when we have discussed bills dealing with changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act, in particular Bill C-69, and I have heard the hon. member prod the government for changes to the act along the lines which the minister has brought forward this afternoon. It is all right for those who come from areas of high employment to take a very scathing look at people who are on unemployment insurance, but those people are always in deprived regions of our country. It is easy to be moralistic about those who are collecting and those who have a minor attachment to the work force.
However, for the purpose of my remarks regarding Bill C-27, I think it is convenient for us to look at its proposals in three major parts. The first deals with the so-called reorganization of unemployment and immigration. The second part deals with the substantive changes in the Unemployment Insurance Act, and they are those which change the minor attachment period from eight weeks to twelve weeks and deal with the length of time during which benefits are paid to claimants. The third part deals with housekeeping amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act.
With regard to the first major change proposed in Bill C-27, namely, the unification of the Department of Manpower and Immigration and the UIC to form the Canada employment and immigration commission with what the minister calls "a small, supporting department," hon. members will instantly recognize that this attempt is similar to what happened in the past with all the king's horses and all the king's men. However, there is one significant difference. In this case the people who took Humpty-Dumpty apart are exactly the same people who now are going to put him together again.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext: And he will be scrambled in the process.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
He will be scrambled in the process. But what was being said in 1965 and 1966, when the government and all its agencies were calling for separation of the national employment service from the Unemployment Insurance Commission, as recommended in the Gill report after an inquiry into the Unemployment Insurance Act? As a result of that report, the national employment service was transferred to the Department of Labour in 1965 and to the Department of Manpower and Immigration in 1966.
The separation of the Unemployment Insurance Commission from the national employment service and its corresponding department was called for on the ground that the national employment service was for too long considered and adjunct and rather subordinate to the insurance plan. The effectiveness of the national employment service in terms of a national manpower policy was being hampered by its ties to the Unemployment Insurance Commission. The two had to be separated so that the national employment service could occupy a leading position in the efforts to solve unemployment problems.
February 1, 1977

Without such a separation there would continue to be an overlapping of efforts and an inadequate provision of staff, facilities and services for the national employment service. We know what resulted from the time of separation to the present. We in this party argued against that dismemberment. We opposed the split of the Unemployment Insurance Commission and the Department of Manpower and Immigration.
We said at that time that no government could look at unemployment without looking at employment in tandem: they could not be looked at separately. But it took this government 11 years to discover that. The government proceeded with the split and began building two empires, with two commissions, two advisory councils, two parallel staffs operating in total isolation in Sudbury, for example, as in many cities. The Canada Manpower offices in Sudbury are hidden in downtown Sudbury, while the offices of the Unemployment Insurance Commission are isolated in suburbia and are inacessible by public transportation. The results are Towers of Babel, built at exorbitant cost to the taxpayer, that are just a holding action against rising unemployment-and in some cases not even that.
What does the Minister of Manpower and Immigration say now? In the document entitled "Highlights and Information Papers on the Employment and Immigration Reorganization Act" he says:
This proposal would produce a new organization capable of providing a one stop service to clients and would facilitate a more integrated approach to the planning and administration of employment, unemployment and immigration programs in Canada.
How wonderful, Mr. Speaker! How much is this reorganization to cost taxpayers, and what about all the back-scratching and in-fighting that has already started as these two units are put together again? What effect will that have on the morale of the departments and, ultimately, on the quality of service to the unemployed? We ask these questions because it is very important to consider what is taking place in putting these monoliths together. We can see the problems. Look at what they have put before us. We can see this minister and his bureaucrats wrapping themselves around organizational charts, beautiful flow charts, an experimental unit and pilot projects, to the exclusion of our most pressing problem- unemployment. They have their little plots and charts in the boardrooms, while the unemployed lines grow.
The second aspect of Bill C-27 which I should like to discuss is the substantive changes which affect minor attachments to the work force, a new benefit structure, and something called "developmental use of unemployment insurance funds." There are times, Mr. Speaker, when one wonders if this House is not a cuckoo's nest. This is one such occasion. The minister proposes a change in the minor attachment period from eight to twelve weeks. Since the May, 1976, budget the minister has run around the country throwing out figures here and there to show that people affected by this change are what he calls kids and housewives.
Employment and Immigration

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext: An insult to the adults of this country.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
That is right. His most recent argument is that the eight to eleven week people are cheaters: they take their benefits until they run out, then take a job for another eight weeks and collect again. I am not surprised at the position taken by the hon. member for Hamilton West. He wants to suck and blow at the same time, and represent to the Atlantic provinces and such places that the Tories are concerned about their unemployment plight; but at the same time he has to satisfy the other parts of Canada which think the unemployment insurance scheme is a disincentive to work.
As far back as May 28, 1975, when the hon. member was in committee with me and we were discussing Bill C-69, he raised the question of going from eight weeks to twelve weeks with the then minister of manpower and immigration, who is now President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras). The minister replied:
I think it is a bit of a red herring myself. I think there are other areas that have to be tidied up in the act that are far more significant than that favourite whipping boy the short term work claimant.
I think it is appropriate for the present minister to know that, so that there can be some continuity. In response to the whole question of laziness of minor attachment claimants which the hon. member for Hamilton West raised in committee, here is what the former minister said:
If you examine where those short term attachment people are, you will find that they coincide with areas of this country that have the more chronic conditions of high unemployment. . . they occur in Quebec and the Atlantic provinces to a higher degree because the conditions of disparity there are such, that people get marginal jobs, which are almost coincidental with short term attachment jobs ... so I think we have to be extremely careful before we tamper with this.
He was referring to the qualifying period. Later in that meeting, in response to the hon. member and his Tory colleagues on the question of the minor attachment claimants being cheaters, the former minister said:
The incidence of disentitlement or disqualification, as an effect of failure to meet one's obligations under the act, is lower amongst the group with a minor attachment to the work force as their proportion of the total claims load than those with a long term attachment to the work force.
When we consider this particular amendment, we must ask: Who are these minor attachment claimants? Are they the kids and the housewives that the minister has alluded to? Where are they located? Is it Hamilton West, Lambton, or where? The figures for the first three months of 1976, which are the only figures available at this time from the department, show that 62 per cent of all unemployment insurance recipients who had worked eight to eleven weeks are located in the Atlantic provinces and Quebec. To show the importance of short-term work in the Atlantic region, the figures reveal that of all recipients in the first three months of 1976, 21 per cent had been able to get work for only eight to eleven weeks. In contrast, the figure was 11 per cent in Ontario, 10 per cent in the prairies, 14 per cent in British Columbia and 15.6 per cent in Quebec.
To reinforce that even further, on a recent visit to Newfoundland, members of this party learned from the United
