Allied Fishermen's Union of Newfoundland that last year, of
1.000	fish plant members in three or four communities from St. Anthony to Twillingate, 400 got less than 12 weeks employment, 200 got less than 16 weeks, and the rest less than 20 weeks. Unemployment Insurance Commission officials in St. John's told us that 48 per cent of all claimants in Newfoundland had between eight and nineteen weeks of contributions.
Mr. Speaker, we know where the minor attachment claimants are, and we should now look at who they are. The government estimates that with an unemployment rate of 7 per cent, 330,000 people will be eliminated from receiving the benefits with the increases in the qualifying period to 12 weeks. According to the government's own estimates, the
330.000	will break down as follows: under 20 years of age,
64.000	people; 20 to 24, 96,000; 25 to 34, 74,500; 35 to 44, 41,000; 45 to 54, 35,000; 55 to 64, 19,000; male, 214,000, and female 116,000. To listen to the minister and his advisers- his lackeys-in the department, the minor attachment claimants are kids and housewives. The facts show that it "ain't so", Mr. Speaker. I wish the minister would stop making these allusions across the country, because they are nothing but false rhetoric.
Let me make another interesting point. In June, 1976, a month when many students were on the job market and unemployed in large numbers, only 12.5 per cent of unemployment insurance recipients, according to the minister, were kids under 20 years of age. Adult women made up 41.7 per cent of all recipients, and adult men 45.8 per cent. Also, what about the myth that unemployed women receiving UIC payments really do not need them? That myth has been bandied about by both major parties in this House. They say that so many of these housewives are working for pin-money.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext: They are married either to economists or civil servants, if one believes the major parties.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Let me deal with the myth which says that unemployed women receiving UIC benefits do not need those benefits. Consider the facts which are supplied by the minister's own department. In August, 1976, Statistics Canada published a study of unemployment in 1973 and 1971. It was found that in both years unemployed wives tended to come from families with low incomes. For example, in 1973 the unemployment rate for all wives was 13.5 per cent; for those from families with incomes between $4,000 and $6,999 the rate was 21.4 per cent, and for those from families with incomes over $15,000 it was 8.6 per cent. As we might suspect, unemployment among low-income women was a real problem. The women in $4,000 to $6,999 group contributed 22 per cent of the family's income when they were working. The women in the $15,000 and up category contributed only 17 per cent. To add salt to the wound, so to speak. Bill C-27, in simplifying the benefit structure to a three-stage arrangement, will cut back the amount of benefits to most recipients. Again, this change will have dire effects on areas of high unemployment.

I was interested to hear the hon. member for Hamilton West delineating the amendment his party wishes the House to consider. Unfortunately, either he did not read it or did not take advice on that part of the bill the amendment seeks to change, because his party's proposal is discriminatory as well. Let me give some examples. In Nova Scotia, a person who has worked 20 weeks would get 51 weeks of benefit under the present system; that is to say, he would have contributed for 20 weeks and would collect unemployment benefits for 51 weeks. If Bill C-27 in its present form were to pass, the person who has worked 20 weeks would get one week of benefit for every week of contribution. He would not get extended benefits because he had not worked for 25 weeks or more.
As well, he could get the regional unemployment benefit, which is paid for a maximum of another 20 weeks. That person will get 40 weeks of benefits, not the 50 weeks which the minister indicated. The minister suggested that such a person would lose a maximum of one week's benefit, his benefit time being reduced from 51 weeks to 50 weeks. I suggest it is not so. That would not be an isolated case, since in many areas of this country it is difficult to secure eight weeks of employment, let alone 20 weeks.
Surely the government ought to consider these things with some heart. Do not tell me that you are going to put all these people to work under the Canada Works program. Surely you are not going to put them all on training programs. It is apparent, from the government's mentality, that it prefers to have large numbers of trained or retrained unemployed to large numbers of untrained unemployed. I suspect that it has bastardized the manpower retraining program in order to keep people off the unemployment rolls. Mr. Speaker, these programs will never work unless the government is committed to a philosophy of full employment. Otherwise, you will be training people for non-existent jobs, and by the time you have trained them, what few jobs existed will have disappeared.
If it were not so sad, I would laugh when I tell hon. members that every second person in Sudbury on manpower retraining is retraining to become a stationary engineer. We shall have so many stationary engineers in the Sudbury basin that we shall be able to man every furnace and boiler from Vancouver Island to Newfoundland with a stationary engineer. I suspect that we have trained too many hairdressers in Newfoundland to fill hairdressing jobs. Consequently, they are again retraining all the hairdressers they trained in Newfoundland, only this time they will turn them into heavy machine operators. Once that process has been finished and there are no jobs for the retrained people, the department will put them through the mill again.
The C. D. Howe Institute has had much to say about manpower retraining programs. They say such programs will not be effective unless there are jobs for the retrained. In the absence of jobs, the program becomes another income support program. Surely that is a very expensive and dehumanizing way to provide income for people.
We ought to consider the impact on the economy of this country of this bill. Surely we cannot cut off those 330,000
February 1, 1977

people who are considered "a minor attachment". Let us remember that the money paid out as unemployment insurance benefits by and large flows into disadvantaged areas of the country. Surely the minister recognizes that the effect of this bill will be to cut off income for certain areas of the country. Let us consider that for a moment. The minister has talked about a saving next year of SI 10 million in UIC benefits. I notice that certain hon. members have talked about a saving of $110 million. That is a nice, round figure. I suppose people say, "Just look at that tough minister; he is really cracking down on unemployment insurance." But the minister never talks about people's lives which will be affected by this measure. Unfortunately, the unemployed become statistics in the minister's mind because he only talks about the $110 million in savings.
The minister also forgets that that is the government's share. That figure does not take into account the employer and employee contributions which amount to between $275 million and $325 million. That much less will be contributed when the amendments before the House come into effect. We learned last Friday, from the reply to an order paper question set down by the hon. member for Hamilton West, what effect these proposed amendments would have had, in 1976, on the economy of Newfoundland, for example. The loss to the economy of Newfoundland would have been between $24 million and $28 million. Is the minister saying that he will pump as much as $28 million into the economy of Newfoundland through Canada Works and Young Canada Works programs? The loss to Nova Scotia would have been between $9 million and $11 million. Those are the government's own figures. New Brunswick would have lost between $ 19 million and $22 million, and Quebec between $93 million and $109 million. Mr. Speaker, the economies of those provinces are fragile and taking that much money out of them will have disastrous effects. That is why I suggested earlier in my remarks that the government should be charged with aggravated assault. One has only to note the effect of this measure on the lives of the people.
A recently published study in the United States showed what unemployment did to the unemployed. Among the unemployed the suicide rate was higher than the national average, as was the incidence of crimes of violence. That ought to concern the minister, but obviously it does not. The government's philosophy is this: if you cannot introduce policies which will stimulate the economy, you do the next best thing, cut some people off unemployment insurance. He is a pretty tough minister. With Bill C-69 we saw how tough the government was with the elderly. Now the minister is getting tough with children and housewives, to use his words. It is a pretty brave government that gets tough with old people, children and housewives.
I listened to the comments made by the hon. member for Hamilton West. One of the Tory spokesmen on manpower and immigration, the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp), is reported in an interview in the Montreal Star of January 13, 1977, as having said as follows:
Employment and Immigration
As a result of questions raised in his constituency, Mr. Epp said, he issued a statement that the party will support the increase from eight to 12 weeks before an applicant can qualify for UIC benefits.
"It is my personal view that the 12 weeks should be increased to levels in the former UIC program of 20 weeks. It is evident the changes are necessary and the government should be commended for introducing these changes, which will result in a saving of $110 million per year," he said.
The hon. member is from Manitoba, which has low unemployment because it is run by an NDP government. Here we have a coalition. Suddenly, 12 weeks is not enough; it should be increased to 20. That is the approach taken in this House. If the government were to be replaced by the official opposition there is nothing to indicate there would be any change. All they would do would be to get tougher and increase it to more than 12 weeks.
There is another myth which this government and the Tories propagate, namely, that the government is going broke because it has to support the unemployment insurance fund. What are the facts? In 1975, when unemployment stood at 7.1 per cent, the unemployment insurance account produced a surplus of $321 million after pay-outs of $3.1 billion in benefits. This year, the government has reduced its share of the cost of UIC from 54 per cent to 38 per cent, thanks to Bill C-69. This year, the UIC fund has done so well that the government is suspending an anticipated increase in employer-employee contributions or premiums scheduled for January 1, 1977-a saving of $250 million to contributors.

It seems to be a half-baked idea that was thrown together. Underemployment is not the solution to long-term, aggravated unemployment. It is fairly obvious that the government's thrust for an employment policy is worksharing. That will not handle all the problems. Incidentally, it smacks of what used to be called "on the job training". We all know how Manpower and the taxpayers of this country were

Adjournment Motion
ripped off by unscrupulous employers in that program. This program is open to abuse.
The job-creation program is something else. That is really creative! Voluntary work on federal government work projects will be available to UIC recipients. They do not have to take that work. It will be on a voluntary basis. Can you imagine any worth-while project being completed? If a person does not want to work on a certain day, he does not have to do so. He may not want to work for two or three days. This is absolutely crazy. Policing will be required. If a recipient of unemployment insurance goes on a job, he is not available to look for work. Under the Unemployment Insurance Act, he has to be available, capable of working and looking for work. If a person is on a voluntary job, somebody will have to say that he is looking for work. But is he? A whole bureaucracy will be required to police these people. The minister knows it will not work. He has just thrown this together to give the impression that the bureaucrats in the Manpower offices are doing some creative thinking.
What about training? From 1970-71 to 1974-75 the manpower department spent up to 75 per cent of its annual budget on manpower training. How much more can they spend on manpower training-100 per cent? Where has this gotten us? As I said before, we are recycling hairdressers in Newfoundland into heavy machine operators. If this government takes a hard, close look at the regions of this country, it will see there are programs that can be carried on effectively.

speechtext:
that Bill C-217, to amend the Railway Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications.
[DOT] (UOO)
He said: Mr. Speaker, I wish to speak briefly on this bill which has certainly been a long time coming. I think I first introduced it some four years ago and I am happy that finally it has percolated through the parliamentary process to this stage, and I hope it will make some further progress. I should like to point out to the House its importance to the safety of life and limb along the roughly 50,000 miles of railroad rights-of-way that criss-cross this country, often bisecting or otherwise cutting through communities. I also want to say at the outset that I firmly believe such a piece of legislation is long overdue.
First of all, the sole purpose of this bill is to amend the Railway Act to provide a better standard, a modern standard, shall we say, of fencing for railroad rights-of-way in the residential areas of Canada's urban municipalities. At present the Railway Act calls for fences of a minimum height of four feet six inches on each side of the railway. Today, as it has been practically since day one of railroading in Canada, that is the only requirement of railway fencing along the right of way. This may have been appropriate as a fencing standard in 1891,
February 1, 1977

or even 50 years ago when railway fences were designed to keep cattle from straying on to the tracks. But it is far from adequate in the 1970s for the proper protection of human life and limb in built-up residential areas across the nation. I am thinking particularly of children. In one location that I know of, two children have been killed by trains in recent years, one in 1967 and another in 1972, because fences were easily climbed, broken down or cut through on railway properties.
We all know as parents and, in some cases, as grandparents, that kids will be kids. They wander. They take short-cuts. They explore. They climb fences and cross barriers simply because they are there, because such obstacles stand between the explorer and the explorable, between the fascinated and the forbidden. From the child's point of view, a fence hinders adventure. But adventures in railway properties too often become shocking misadventures, if not tragedies, for the curious or thrill-seeking child, or even for the youngster trying to find a short-cut to and from school.
Some of us in this House may recall what fun it was leaping from boxcar to boxcar, running across the roof-walks, hanging from the grab-irons, fiddling with immovable couplings or rummaging in and among empty, open cars. But those of us who may be able to remember the fun of fooling around in a freight yard may also have some bad memories of injuries to ourselves or to our playmates.
There is danger enough among rolling-stock that is not rolling, amidst monstrous steel cars that stand stock still, rusting in the rain, roasting in summer sunshine. But the real danger is in poorly fenced track, in places where the rolling-stock is rolling, where diesels and switchers move suddenly and without warning, dangers that only the trained, experienced railroad worker can recognize and react to in safety. Where the trains move near homes and schools, parks or playgrounds, there is sudden and swift tragedy lurking for the unwary, for the innocent child who may not even realize he is trespassing, let alone flirting with death or dismemberment.
Today there are so many more built-up areas near longstanding railroad tracks than there were when the section of the Railway Act which my bill would amend was drafted and legislated. The concern then, 85 years ago, was for the safety of cattle. Today we are, hopefully, more concerned about the safety of people and, most of all, I would hope, the safety of children. Today there are so many more children and others apt to stray on to railroad property because it is so easy to do, with only 4V4 feet of fencing standing in their way-if in fact it is standing there at all and not falling down, or simply non-existent.
A mere 54 inches stands between safety and danger, at best. Fifty-four inches of wire fencing is nothing to any individual who is curious enough, determined enough, or even stupid enough to climb on to a railway right-of-way, for whatever purpose. But you put up a chain-link fence at least six feet in height, and there you have a formidable obstacle, a solid safety factor, one which could well save many an adventurous child the pain and the agony of being crushed between the steel
Railway Fencing
wheels of trains on the move-and some trains move at a pretty fair clip, even through residential areas.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, the amendment to the Railway Act which Bill C-217 proposes is this:
Her Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada, enacts as follows:
"1. Paragraph 214(1 )(a) of the Railway Act is repealed and the following substituted therefor:
(a) fences of a minimum height of four feet six inches on each side of the railway and in residential areas of incorporated municipalities having a population in excess of 3,000, such fences shall be of a chain link construction with a minimum height of six feet, the maintenance and quarterly inspection of which is the sole responsibility of the company."
Let me repeat what I said in the beginning, what I have said time and time again since I began trying to get action on this matter four years ago. We are concerned here with saving lives, young lives, not of cattle but of human beings. We should be concerned also that this matter has gone virtually without major public support for far too long and lives have been lost in the meantime. Lives have been lost that need not have been in jeopardy at all. I believe this is a worth-while amendment, otherwise I would not have brought it to the attention of the House and imposed upon this chamber's time. I believe this amendment to the Railway Act is a good move, a most sensible move in terms of public safety.
While it is always nice to have support for one's proposal, I hope I do not get too much support that will cause the hour to expire before some action is taken on what I consider to be a very reasonable suggestion, one that should receive the serious consideration of the legislative process and not just fall to the bottom of the list when the hour today expires.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING HEIGHT OF RIGHT-OF-WAY FENCING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would be very happy to have the question put, and I certainly will not speak for very long. I was impressed with the hon. member's remarks in introducing this amendment; it is one with which I heartily agree. I have been very concerned, as I am sure have other members, about areas where there are railway crossings. I think particularly of one area in Ottawa, not far from here, where the railway passes through a very heavily built-up part of town, and they are still using the old type of fence, actually the same old fence. The fence was probably put up 30 to 40 years ago and there does not seem to be any desire to maintain or to meet changing requirements.
Originally, the law requiring railways to provide fencing on both sides of the railway track stemmed from a very simple necessity: animals such as cows, wild animals and domestic, would run on the track, and I presume fencing was originally put up by the railway as a protection against liability. I should like to add that in my opinion, in addition to proper fencing, particularly in built-up areas, an immediate attempt should be made to provide barriers, lights or other kinds of marking, rather than a signpost back 15 to 20 feet from the railway track, especially where a railway track crosses a major highway. This is true in my area where there have been a number of fatalities at a crossing which was unmarked or was very poorly marked and there was a very heavy amount of traffic crossing the track. Your Honour had the opportunity at being

Railway Fencing
at the other end of the problem, as it were, behind the throttle, and I am sure you will agree with me that the locomotive cannot compete with an automobile when it comes to yielding the right of way.
The automobile can stop in a short distance. Trains, especially heavily laden trains, cannot do so in most cases. Many fatalities at railway crossings might have been prevented had the necessary action been taken. We pass legislation making the construction of overpasses the subject of negotiations in communities over years and years. I do not think there has ever been an overpass or an underpass built except in cases where a number of fatalities had already taken place at that point.
The CN and the CP run through my area for 200 or 300 miles, but the railway which I am most familiar with is the Ontario Northland which travels the full length of my constituency. Its solution has been to close off the crossings. However, in consideration of this proposal it is interesting to note that when they close off these crossings all they do is put up a couple of posts in the middle of the road: they put up a couple of planks and leave the road there. Usually the young people drive through before they are convinced the road is closed. Never does the railway put up a fence which really prevents youths from using the road as a crossing point.
It has been the practice of Ontario Northland to close crossings when there is difficulty. If an accident occurs, the result will likely be that they close the road, with the result that the neighbouring township has to build considerably more road to provide a crossing somewhere else. But the railway does not put up an installation of the type the hon. member suggests. Had this been done, at least 15 lives would have been saved in my area alone in the last four or five years. If this is representative of the situation in other ridings across the country, I strongly urge that an amendment of the type suggested be passed.
There must be a major rethinking of our legislation if we are to see the type of link fence comparable to the fencing we find in cities, for example, around hydro facilities or anything else which presents a major danger to young adults. The railway companies should be pressed to consider the installation of such fencing in all areas. It would not be the kind of fencing railroads are now required to provide. It would be a new type which would be child proof, which could not be scaled and which would largely eliminate the danger to which the hon. member has called attention.
I have in mind the safety of children whose parents live in suburbs close to a railway where trains often pass at considerable speed. Perhaps the danger is greatest in those areas where not many trains pass during the day and where, as a result, parents are often not as diligent as they otherwise might be in supervising their children.
It is possible that the provision of adequate restraining fences would call for municipal money as well as for railway money. Nevertheless, I think the idea is well worth consider-
[Mr. Peters.)
ing. I hope the House approves this amendment so that the railways will begin taking this problem seriously and do something about it.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING HEIGHT OF RIGHT-OF-WAY FENCING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I must congratulate the mover of this bill concerning railway fencing. I think this question has not been dealt with for a long time because, according to the law, only 4 foot 6 inch fences are needed. That would be all right in rural areas because, along the tracks in my region which is 90 per cent rural, fences are generally well maintained, even though it is especially difficult for the CN during winter to keep those fences in top shape as snowdrifts have knocked them down over many miles. In springtime the railways companies have to spend much money to put up again their fences. But I do not believe it would be necessary to require that those fences be 6 or 7 feet out in the country.
This bill deals with fencing in urban areas. Here again, I would favour 4 foot fences even though the bill specifies 8 feet 6 inches but that depends on the type of fences, Mr. Speaker. If the bill refers to existing fences, those which are put up according to the law, they will be proposed in the cities, but they will not represent an obstacle for children. So we must discuss the type of fences and I think that should be done by the Committee on Transport and Communications.
I think that what is needed is at least an 8 foot barbed-wire topped steel fence because the usual small fence with large squares would not prevent children from going through and playing on the railroads.
I think that we must inform the people. The best fence is child education. We must teach the children that the railway is a public road, just like the highway. We very rarely see children playing on a regional road. The previous speaker, the spokesman for the Progressive Conservatives, said earlier that the lack of fences causes fatalities, but let us not forget that fatalities can also be caused by cars when children are not careful enough and play on the roadway. But this is no excuse for the railroads.
If we want to talk about the quality of fences to be put in cities, let us talk about fences that will not completely disfigure a city.
Railway crossings ouside and even within city limits where there are no signals are another problem which should be submitted to the Committee on Transport and Communications. I have already talked in the House about these railway crossings where there are no signals. It is a fact that the signals exist on interprovincial roads, but in rural centres, there are many secondary roads with little or no signals.
In my opinion, this is a bill aimed at protecting everyone. This matter should be submitted to the committee. But to come back to the bill, as concerns fences to be put up in cities along railways tracks, I believe this is a very important matter since we cannot take too many precautions to protect the life of children, and even if the only result of the bill was to draw the attention of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) to the

matter for it to be referred to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications where it can at least be studied so that something can finally be done about a type of fence which would be appropriate for the cities, the hon. member will not have lost his time and we could give the population of our regions a much better safety device to protect the children.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to join in this debate this afternoon on the bill introduced by the hon. member for Palliser (Mr. Schumacher) in which he points out another area of the social responsibility of the railways to the Canadian public. In effect, he is touching on an over-all area which is of interest to me, not by design but more by accident owing to circumstances in the area I represent in metropolitan Toronto.
Here we are talking about a question of the adequacy of safety factors that are designed to prevent people from having access to the railroad tracks, which is quite desirable. In another instance, when we talk grade level separations, as referred to by one of the other speakers this afternoon, we are referring to the need for adequate safety factors in order to prevent collisions between trains and vehicular traffic. In both cases I am personally not at all convinced that the railroads, the municipalities or even the provincial or federal government have given sufficient attention over the years to the hazards that exist.
I was most impressed this summer in England, on an automobile trip that took us perhaps not more than 250 or 300 miles from north of London down to the south coast, to notice that in not one case did we traverse a railroad track at a level crossing. In other words, every single crossing was graded. I mentioned this in the course of a conversation with my companion who has lived in England all his life and I asked him how this came to be. He said it was really simple, because in that country when the railway came into existence many of the towns and the people populating them were there, so the railways had to conform to their wishes. In other words, they were bringing something new to the country and they had to conform with regard to safety factors such as those relating to fencing, level crossings, etc.
We see the exact opposite on this continent and certainly in this country where the railways in many cases constituted the first signs of any major spurt of civilization to appear in many areas. So the railways tended to have things going their own way. Unfortunately, this may have been satisfactory in the latter part of the nineteenth century and in the first part of the twentieth century, but is not satisfactory today and I do not think the Canadian public are prepared to accept this situation in the future.
I noted, in the few minutes that were available to me prior to speaking this afternoon, that the municipality of metropolitan Toronto has appealed to the federal government regarding the matter of adequacy or inadequacy of fencing. I believe that
Railway Fencing
resolutions came forward as recently as 1974 in which metro Toronto was asking for a review of the situation.
I understand that the costs involved in what the hon. member for Palliser has suggested would be exorbitant. Nevertheless, it seems to me that the problem is there and that it must be addressed. I would like to think it will be addressed in conjunction with this over-all question of the adequacy of safety factors in urban areas. At present I am working with the CTC on this very problem. We cannot build quickly grade separations in Scarborough. This is, incidentally the responsibility of municipalities with substantial federal financial backing. We cannot quickly build the 35 grade separations that are needed over the foreseeable future, because 16 of the most urgent alone will cost $69 million. Therefore, we are forced to look immediately at the whole question of the adequacy of existing safety factors. I suggest that this safety factor at level crossings is just another extension, or vice versa, of safety factors that the hon. member is talking about in relation to people having undesirable access to the tracks.
There is another matter in relation to the responsibility of the railways in this country which should be mentioned, and that is the basic need for the railway companies-which, after all, are nothing more or less than a form of public utility-to respond more adequately to the concerns of people. Particularly in our modern urban situation the kind of responses they might have given even 20 years ago are not acceptable today.
When I was speaking in the debate on my own bill, C-20, on the need to have the railways go before the CTC for approval of additional marshalling yards, I used the example of an individual in an urban area who must go to his municipality for approval to build even the most minor structure in his backyard. I think I can bring out the hon. member's point today with the analogy of the home owner who wishes to build a swimming pool. He has an obligation, in most urban areas today, to fence that swimming pool adequately. In fact, in some urban areas the requirements are much greater than in others. This is done for one reason only, simply to ensure that access to that swimming pool will not be obtained by children or others who may be wandering around.
I do not know what the size of the fence should be, nor what its quality should be in order to preclude undesirable access to railway tracks, but I have a great deal of sympathy for the suggestion that we at least re-examine the responsibility of the railroads in this entire area.
I receive submissions from my municipality about the manner in which rights-of-way are maintained; about the fact that weeds are allowed to grow and in many cases the area in general is kept in an undesirable state. So I certainly support the proposal put forward by the hon. member. I presume it would ultimately require the Canadian Transport Commission to at least assess the adequacy of fencing in urban areas. I do not personally know whether it is now adequate or inadequate but I am prepared to believe the review made by the hon. member.
Another area of safety that should be considered is that involved in bridges. There have been examples of children

Railway Fencing
being caught on these bridges. In our own area last year two youngsters were so caught and had no chance to escape and were killed. I believe that one fell off and was drowned in the river beneath. Concerns in this area are extremely important.
I wonder if the government should not insist that the Canadian Transport Commission, which, after all, is the regulatory body charged by the government with the responsibility of overseeing railroad operations, take very seriously the submissions which are made to it by members of the public and by members of parliament who are after all acting on behalf of members of the public. In my view, the CTC should consider these areas of major concern. The commission should consider the adequacy of safety at level crossings which remain unprotected, and probably will continue to remain unprotected well into the future. It should also consider the question of speeds of trains through urban areas. That is another important factor. The manual may indicate that a train can proceed at 50 miles an hour through an urban area; that may have been fine 30 years ago, but it might not be fine today. Today there may be tens of thousands of people living in this same area and 50 miles an hour may simply be too fast a speed.
Warning devices in train cabs may be needed to help detect any vehicles that may be caught at level crossings. Perhaps more adequate fencing is needed to prevent undesirable access to tracks. It seems to me that there must be an over-all change in the attitude of the railroads toward their social responsibility. I quite agree that the railroads must perform specific services. They must transport people and goods efficiently and quickly. There is no question about that, but I think they also have social and community responsibilities just as hydro companies do with their electricity distribution; just as natural gas companies do with their natural gas pipelines; and oil companies with their related pipelines. The railroads have a responsibility to ensure that in the course of providing their services they indeed bear in mind concerns about noise pollution and these other very real concerns, whether they be with regard to urban areas or other areas, but particularly in the case of heavily populated urban areas where so many of the current problems prevail.
I have not had an opportunity in the very short time available to me to examine all the ramifications of what the hon. member has in mind, but I can easily and wholeheartedly support the concept of the need for a review by the Canadian Transport Commission at this time of the adequacy of the fencing situation, together with the adequacy of other safety factors relating to the over-all operation of railroads in our urban areas.

speechtext:
I am glad that the distinguished hon. member for Palliser corrected me. I have, of course, the French version, and it in fact says eight feet six inches. I suppose the hon. member means a fence with a minimum height of six feet. I read somewhere that fences are to be climbed, and starting from this point of view-

Fences are there to be climbed. I wonder what would be the reaction of the public in general, youngsters who are tempted to jump the current 4 foot six inch high fence provided for by the agreement between the Department of Transport and the municipalities. Section 214 which has been quoted reflects the existing agreement with municipalities wherein there is provision for joint programs with municipalities for the construction of fences.
The security of passengers as well as that of children is of the utmost importance, Mr. Speaker. I believe that my hon. colleague is indeed endeavouring to bring about such a protection. However, as my colleague, the hon. member for Scarborough West (Mr. Martin) has indicated, I hesitate to think of the cost of replacing the 4 foot six inch fence by a security system providing for a maximum height of six feet since there are indeed places where it would be necessary to raise the height of the fences. On the other hand, in certain other places, it would not perhaps be as necessary for railway companies to build fences if we consider the terrain, whether it is hilly, very isolated, without any houses in a ten mile radius, so perhaps it is less urgent for railway companies to build fences.
What we may have neglected in this matter is instructing our children on the respect of other people's property. They must learn that by trespassing on other people's property, it is as if they were in fact robbing their neighbour and it would perhaps not be necessary to introduce such restrictive measures if schools or families imposed a stricter discipline to prevent youngsters from jumping fences and trespassing on private property.
Mr. Speaker, there is only one railway line, Canadian Pacific, linking Montreal to the higher Laurentians, at Mont Laurier, cutting through my region and there exists already, as I have already indicated, an agreement with the municipalities it crosses, therefore I do not think it necessary to build a six foot fence along that line all the way from Montreal to Mont Laurier.
Perhaps when we give a new structure to our public transport system, it might be necessary to find a new design for our
February 1, 1977

railway tracks, especially on the section between Montreal and Mont-Laurier, and to use lighter and faster equipment, with new faster acceleration and deceleration devices. This would reduce the risk of accidents and in case of an animal, an adult or a child crossing the railway track, lighter equipment and a safer deceleration system would allow a far better control of the engine.
But I think it might not be worth investing in equipment which is not that necessary. A few years ago someone introduced a bill to relocate railway tracks within municipal jurisdictions. This relocation program might then give railway companies the opportunity to build new, safer and stronger fences which would make any trespassing much more difficult.
But outside this program, I do not see the interest for railways companies to assume an additional expense which as someone put it earlier with the number of railway tracks existing in our country could represent several million dollars. This would be an excessively expensive item and I wonder if we should not wait until this relocation program is applied and take the opportunity then to repair or rebuild new fences.
These are the arguments I wanted to put forward, Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING HEIGHT OF RIGHT-OF-WAY FENCING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Palliser (Mr. Schumacher) raised a question relating to Bill C-217, namely whether the improvement of fences along railroad tracks would reduce the number of accidents recorded each year. Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate the hon. member for his excellent initiative and I also want to take this opportunity to thank and congratulate all hon. members who participated in this important debate relating to the bill that the hon. member introduced.
All hon. members have very commendable intentions, and once again let me say that this is especially the case of the hon. member for Palliser. They show that the members are deeply concerned with the matter protecting not only adults but also and especially children. On the other hand, many of the municipalities that the members who took part in the debate mentioned have built miles of fences, especially at trouble spots, in collaboration with railway companies. In some cases however, the railway companies only paid for the usual fences necessary for the protection of the public and the municipalities concerned paid for the difference. In other words, this means that the companies are willing to go along with the municipalities if they want to build such fences.
It is difficult however for the railway companies to pay the total cost of such fences, especially when you know the huge amount of money necessary for such a measure. On the other hand, this situation could create a dangerous precedent if it were applied in various areas of the country.
I think that the systematic building of fences along the railroad tracks is not possible at the present time for the following reasons.
Railway Fencing
The basic question on the proposed Bill C-217 is whether improved fencing would in fact provide a higher level of protection against pedestrian accidents on railway property. At a number of urban locations throughout Canada arrangements between railway companies and municipalities have led to the installation of chain link fencing of the type suggested. The experience in these locations has indicated that while the fences serve the purpose of warning that danger exists, fences alone have not prevented trespassing. Fencing is open at each level crossing and trespassers have ample access at these points to railway rights of way. To some degree, high chain link fencing tends to deflect trespassers along rights of way, as opposed to the direct crossing pattern which exists under the less restrictive type of fencing.
It is not clear that fences, whatever their height, will successfully prevent trespassing on railway rights of way or significantly reduce the potential for injury to pedestrians. Most of the pedestrians killed on railway rights of way by trains are adults who are, of course, fully aware of the dangers of trespassing on railway property. For example, in 1972, 66 pedestrians were killed by trains, and 56 of these were over 16 years of age.

Let me question the very principle of fences along railway lines, as opposed to other modes. Nobody ever thought of installing fences along highways. The danger however is so much greater for a pedestrian to be hit by an automobile than a train. Apparently the public are more aware of the inherent dangers in highway traffic.
The main concern of citizen groups urging for the installation of higher fences along railways is for the safety of children, who do not always realize the danger in crossing tracks. The railroad industry already suggested that children in primary schools should be provided with basic instruction to make them aware of that kind of danger. I believe the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Dupras) already indicated this in his speech. Certainly such a policy would be much more effective than this proposal.
It must be noted Canada's two main railroads have already launched school programs to that effect. The federal government are perfectly aware of this problem, and the Canadian Transport Commission conducts regular reviews in areas where it feels there is room for improvement. We have seen a number of cases where the CTC indicated to the railroad companies that extra protection should be provided. Generally speaking the latter have implemented the commission's recommendations.
In Canada's metropolitan areas we have a very high density and length of trackage, and the cost of installing fences along the roadway would be tremendous. Referring to studies that were conducted in 1972, the installation of six-foot high chain link fences in every municipality over 30,000 population would cost upwards of $100 million. Moreover, the annual mainte-

nance cost of such fences would be so much higher than the current cost of maintaining existing fences. In 1970, the capital outlay required for the installation of metal fences in the city of Toronto alone was estimated at $1,600,000 for a total length of 270,000 feet, and this involved the most dangerous areas only. Assuming this would have to be done in the metropolitan area, the cost would rise tenfold. These studies go back to 1970.
At present the cost would be much higher. It would be extremely difficult to justify this kind of expenditure particularly when we know that safety would not be improved much as a result. And even then in terms of figures let me continue to illustrate the ineffectiveness of a metal fence along a railway track.
Let us now take an example in the city of Ottawa. The Canadian National owns about five miles of fencing starting at the grade separation on Riverside Drive and extending to a level crossing also located on Riverside Drive. That fence was installed by the National Capital Commission and is being maintained now by the Canadian National. There are at present some twenty holes in the fence that were made not by planners but by people wishing to cross the tracks at a place convenient to them.
The job of repairing holes in that fence is given to specialists and is not being done by the maintenance crews of the CN. Repairs to that fence alone cost more than $100 a week, that is about $5,000 a year. The Canadian National also noticed that as soon as a fence is repaired it is nearly automatically reopened the day after.
In addition to the points I already mentioned applications are made from time to time to improve or put up fencing along railway tracks but there is still little evidence that a fence would improve safety or reduce accidents. Finally, the public always manages to get around the difficulties and rather than using the free crossings designed for that purpose it prefers to go over or through fences normally put up to protect them.
The federal government favours improvements in this area. It is doing everything it can to protect the lives of citizens. Hence it is very sympathetic to the ideas and the philosophy expressed in Bill C-217. Unfortunately it does not seem obvious that this bill would actually help improve safety or represent the best investment of public funds to ensure public safety. The government is currently reviewing in its entirety this matter of safety in railway operations. Hopefully that in-depth work will lead to very specific recommendations, as was mentioned by those hon. members who participated in this debate and made specific recommendations concerning the steps to be taken by the government in cooperation with municipalities and the railway industry which, as hon. members mentioned, also has responsibilities in this respect. Following those few remarks concerning the proven financial impracticability and ineffectiveness of such a broad bill the government must regretfully reject it. However, as I mentioned the federal government is now reviewing the whole matter of public safety along railway tracks both in urban areas as well as in certain other places in this country. I think

the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier) also touched on this point. We hope then to be in a position to propose a legislation along those lines in the months to come.
Hon. members have also emphasized the necessity for all municipalities to co-operate with the railway industry, and I feel they are now ready to work hand in hand with the government on this matter.
I should like to mention, however-

In these cases the railway restricted its expenditure to the amount it would expend in the case of normal fencing, and the balance of the cost has been assumed by the city or town in question. In other words the railways are willing to co-operate with the municipalities if it is their wish to install chain link fencing. The railways do not, however, wish to absorb the total cost of chain link fencing, particularly in the face of the large expenditures which could be involved if a precedent were to be set.

All hon. members will doubtless agree that if the federal government were to support such a project, in view of the ineffectiveness of security measures, we could have much more profitable investments.
On behalf of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) I want to thank all those who have taken part in this debate for their positive suggestions. I wish especially to commend the hon. member for Palliser (Mr. Schumacher) who has brought up this important issue and who wishes to amend the Railway Act by adding, and I quote:
"(a) fences of a minimum height of four feet six inches on each side of the railway and in residential areas of incorporated municipalities having a population in excess of 3,000, such fences shall be of a chain-link construction with a minimum height of six feet, the maintenance and quarterly inspection of which is the sole responsibility of the company".
May I assure the hon. member that this bill is highly considered by the authorities of the Department of Transport and particularly by the minister. We can assure him that the government is extremely favourable to this concern with protecting public life adequately, and we suggest to the hon. member, as well as to those who took part in the debate this afternoon, that they continue being concerned about the importance of protecting public interest by ensuring public safety through various means.
Mr. Speaker, I feel that the views expressed here by all hon. members and by the Department of Transport reflect the wishes of the whole population. Mr. Speaker, I believe it is six o'clock. Should I continue my remarks?
