Order, please. The hour appointed for the consideration of private members' business having expired, I do now leave the chair until 8 o'clock p.m.
At six o'clock the House took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 8 p.m.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Cullen that Bill C-27, to establish the Department of Employment and Immigration, the Canada Employment and Immigration Commission and the Canada Employment and Immigration Advisory Council, to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971 and to amend certain other statutes in consequence thereof, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when we broke off at five o'clock this afternoon I was commenting on the so-called development use of unemployment insurance funds as proposed in Bill C-27.
One of the so-called uses of unemployment insurance funds is for training programs. The Conference Board in a recent report noted that we had enough training programs and what we lacked was jobs. This is echoed by Ms. Barbara Goldman of the C. D. Howe Research Institute in a recent study entitled "New Directions for Manpower Policy". Canada gets a real
Employment and Immigration
payoff from training only if the trainees can find steady employment. Otherwise training is simply another form of providing income support.
In the same article, Ms. Goldman quotes Seymour Brand-wein, the Director of the Office of Manpower Program Evaluation, Employment and Training Administration of the United States Department of Labour, as saying in 1976, and I quote:
To the extent that economic growth generates new jobs, training programs should be a tool for developing the skills and performance needed to sustain such growth and for equipping workers of limited skills or other background to fulfil the opportunities offered by such new jobs.
Obviously putting more money into training programs will not eliminate unemployment. The economics of those regions I mentioned earlier will not even keep up with those coming into the work market. When in St. John's, Newfoundland, we learned from the Canada Manpower Centre and UIC officials that, just to keep the Newfoundland unemployment at 13 per cent, the economy of Newfoundland would have to produce 10,000 jobs, yet last year only 5,200 jobs were created.
We learned on that trip to Newfoundland and Cape Breton that there are many specific proposals regarding development of long-term economic opportunities, but they offer no farsighted decision making by the federal government in collaboration with the provinces concerned. Such things as secondary harbours, establishment of marine bases for air and sea rescue, improvement and initiation of transport facilities, primary resource development to final stage, and shipbuilding with specific attention to fishing trawlers and a Canadian commercial fleet, require planning and a commitment to full employment as a basic right of each and every Canadian.
One other housekeeping amendment in Bill C-27 which ought to interest us is the pregnancy benefits amendment. Since clauses 34 and 38 open up this question, an amendment ought to be made which would provide adoptive mothers with the same right to unemployment insurance benefits as is allowed to one who has given birth naturally. This is a discriminatory clause which presently exists and ought to be changed now.
One other matter I would like to deal with is the question of appeals. At the present time there is an automatic right to appeal to an umpire by any worker covered by an organization of workers, a trade union. But a non-represented worker must seek the approval of the chairman of the board of referees. If he has a unanimous decision against him, he may get special approval to go to the umpire. I suspect this is watering down the right of organized workers. Now they all have to get approval of the umpire under certain conditions to have the appeal heard before the umpire. It would be much better if we gave all those who have appealed to the board of referees and who have had a unanimous decision against them an automatic right of appeal to the umpire.
In conclusion, we as a party cannot support those clauses in Bill C-27 that so obviously discriminate against the helpless of our country who have absolutely no influence with regard to public and private economic decision making. We will

seems his job should have been found by the employees of the manpower centre. But they simply cannot get him a job so the man himself, because he has connections-a friend on a working site, a parent-manages to land a job and after making sure-he has got to work for a few weeks at least- after making sure that his job will be permanent he gets in touch with the manpower centre. No, sir, that doesn't work, you did not submit that at the beginning-he did not even know he would find a job at this place.
If a citizen from Sainte-Helene in Kamouraska gets a job in Fort-Captif, 400 miles away from his home on the north shore, or if another one from the same place in Kamouraska wants to get a job in Montreal, 300 miles away from his home, when he leaves home he does not know if he will succeed in finding a job. But he has got to tell the employees of the manpower centre where he goes and, if he finds a job, he will have to leave it temporarily to tell them that he might probably get a job. This system can hardly be applied. In the construction field, how many workers had to suffer from the rules of the construction bureau which wants them to get working permits? Several workers from my area had to pay $200 and $225 fines for the simple reason that they had worked without a permit and that they could not get one for particularly stupid reasons.
I already took action to shorten the sentence of a young man, an 18-year-old student who had been found guilty of nothing more than working with his father on a construction site during his holidays without a working permit. We should not be surprised by the violent reactions that sometimes happen. Patience grows thinner with rigid laws and regulations too often creating more problems that the incentives that would be needed at certain times in life when things get difficult. The end result is that revolt gets the better of people who used to be moderates, and no amount of promises will quiet them down.
When the unemployed lose patience with the finicky administration of the Unemployment Insurance Act which is too complex already, should they be admonished or should they be said the benefits they are entitled to? The time is ill chosen to tell them there was a computation error or their file is dormant. In my view, many civil servants are dormant themselves. Not all of them, but a good number. The unemployed derives no comfort from being told his file will be converted providing there is no problem in the complex computer techniques. That is the kind of answer we get from the Unemployment Insurrance Commission offices.
It is easily seen that the well paid bureaucrats-some are too well paid-who draft the legislation know nothing of the unemployed's position. I looked up the definition of the term "Technocrat" in the dictionary, and this is what I found: "A supporter of technocracy; a politician or high-ranking civil servant exercising authority on the basis of thorough theorical studies of economic mechanisms, without taking sufficient account of human factors." No wonder our Unemployment Insurance Act is not understandable to most unemployed workers. Add to that a deluge of regulations prepared in such
Employment and Immigration
a way as to allow the most inventive civil servants to get at the unemployed at every stage of the application processing. Everyone knows this, we easily realize that everything is aimed at protecting the fund. Rather than helping the unemployed obtain a lucrative job, they are given generous benefits to assure their subsistence and that of their family. Another indication that the protection of the fund is the determining factor is the authority given to income tax officials-those are two teams which do seem to get along rather well-to determine whether a job is insurable.
The legislation is so complex that a team of officials is necessary to establish whether such or such a job is insurable. This transfer of powers proceeds from Bill C-259 passed at the end of 1971 after closure was invoked, one of the most bulky bills to be introduced in the House, having more than 700 pages. It was the result of a ten-year study of so-called improved taxation procedures and that famous bill had to come into effect at the beginning of January 1972.
The taxing authorities had been ordered to be on the alert and put an end to the rip-off and the first to experience the modified system were the unemployed. It is unthinkable but true. Some unemployed who had been waiting for their benefits for months were paid retroactive to January 1972 amounts due in November and December 1971. The computer with all its electronic circuits working deducted from unemployed workers $4, $5, and $6 a week for federal and provincial income tax. What a fine example of cooperative, separatist, leftist and provincialist federalism. All unemployed were taxed as of January 1972.
Of course, UIC officials received numerous phone calls about this method of taxation. Since they already had transitional problems to cope with as a result the new act, I saw fit to point out this fine example of fund protection. There are many others, namely the decision to disentitle people of 65, when most of them had contributed to the fund ever since the act came into force. You must agree with me that the fund was far better protected than the unemployed.
A further example: do we know what happens when a benefit period must be established? Officials must take into account all severance allowances which may have been paid to the worker when he was laid off, as well as special holiday allowances in addition to normal vacation pay to which he is entitled under the act and all bonues or premiums owed to him, since those fringe benefits are considered as income. Consequently the officials shorten the period during which the claimant is eligible for benefits. There again, they are protecting the fund. There are even examples of the UIC reducing the rate of benefit of farmers who had been getting subsidies for "wintering" cattle when the beef market was paralyzed. They are sort of subsidized by the government. The UIC considers this as an income. They have to report it and then their rate of benefit is reduced.
I could go on giving many other examples where the main intention is to save the fund. When we read the sections of the law and the regulations, we find out that those in charge of the administration of the plan have managed to attain their aim,

Employment and Immigration
through the technocrats who write the law; regulations are added when the increased number of unemployed people makes it necessary. One time they decided to summon claimants to the UIC office and prepared non-eligibility notices for those who did not show up on time or on the date they had been called. I often had the opportunity of seeing that both notices were mailed on the same day. This has already hap-penned: anyone who does not report on the day he has been called does not have time to explain why he could not come, the notices are ready, the forms prepared in advance. Then, if your are not there at 11 o'clock, you will receive a notice of disentitlement of six weeks. I intervened with the board of referees a number of times to try and help out unemployed who were held through the system's faults.
Let us take a look now at what is happening when the employee leaves his job. The officials pay attention mostly to reasons given by the employer and the claimant receives a notice of disqualification for six weeks. They do not bother to ask him what are his reasons for leaving, no way. They call the employer on the telephone for additional details. The employee is disqualified for six weeks, he is not entitled to benefits. One would believe that a great number of civil servants are there because there is unemployment, because workers have contributed to the unemployment insurance funds for months and years. These civil servants owe their own job to this very fact.
Unfortunately, with such a bad law, these people have reached a point where they say: This is our fund, we are the ones who should protect it. How many times have I helped out poor workers to clarify this type of decision. It has been established beyond all doubt that the employee had good reasons to leave his job. I do not approve this attitude when reasons are not adequate, but one must not penalize a worker who has good reasons to change jobs.
Since statements of employment are often given too late to the employee, the ensuing loss of income should be charged to the employer. No, nothing in the act provides for that. Naturally, employers issue the statement of employment when the employee leaves, but some employers take weeks and months to do so. Then the commission says: You may file your claim anyway, but you will not be paid until the commission receives the statement of employment. But nothing in the act requires the employer to issue it or to support the unemployed person who has to wait because of his failure to provide the statement of employment.
I shall summarize this part of my speech by quoting a statement made by the former governor of the Bank of Canada, Mr. Rasminsky, which was published in the Quebec City newspaper Le Soleil on March 20, 1971, and I quote:
Unemployment, a necessary evil-Rasminsky
Last Thursday, the Governor of the Bank of Canada warned that Canada should not wage an all-out war against unemployment at the risk of creating further inflation.
He is safe, he has nothing to fear, for he is handsomely paid.

"A margin of security must be maintained in the rate of unemployment", stated Mr. Rasminsky in his annual report to the government. Keeping a large number of unemployed on the labour force is a necessary evil to prevent greater evils, such as an excess demand and the depletion of supplies which would automatically result in price increases.
In a recently published book entitled L'economie du diable, by a French author, I read in a paragraph of Chapter I a short comment on the mirage of unemployment and employmnet, and I quote:
The extreme sensitivity of public opinion to the unemployment curse creates ideal conditions as it were, a sprouting of illusions. Myths, simplistic reasoning, beliefs, mischievous dogmas are second nature to man. Indeed, no other area of investigation succeeds any better in separating the researcher from the rest of mankind. Reality is not only far from, but often contrary to appearances.
Because of a so badly worded Unemployment Insurance Act and the confusion it creates and entertains, a number of civil servants confuse reality with probability. Some appear to have lost all sense of proportions. They know or ought to know that unemployment has reached very high levels in certain areas, but they force victims of unemployment to take useless and sometimes costly steps in search of undiscoverable work, particularly at certain times, of the year. If they were serious, they could consult manpower centres officials: they would be told that they have hundreds of applications in their files and no jobs to offer. Their regulations seem to get their inspiration from a Birman proverb which says: There may not be gold in every stone but there is no harm in looking.
Unemployed people are accused of living at the expenses of workers. Basically, if someone is living at the expenses of workers in our society, is it not rather those who exploit them? Unemployed people are entitled to social benefits. This is not a gift from the government. Unemployed people are entitled to some objective, undisguised information on their situation, on their due. They should not be penalized for the slightest omission. This is not a right, this is something of an attitude taken by civil servants, and I do not know what temper they can have, but there are some among them who are not easy to deal with. The worker is penalized if he deliberately quits his job, even if he is exploited and works under inhuman conditions; the unemployed is penalized if he does not look actively for a job, even if there are no jobs available and if the unemployment rate reaches 30 per cent; the unemployed is penalized if he is not available; he ought to stay at home near the telephone, watching television, listening to the radio, reading the newspaper, always on the look-out for a job. He is penalized if he moves, and moreover, he has to pay his moving expenses. The unemployed pay out of their own money for the operation of the UIC. And if, in spite of all this, mistakes and delays occur, they only have to pay twice. These are more or less the conclusions to be drawn.
Mr. Speaker, I will give the minister an idea of the reaction and I may add that it is fairly general. I used to know a responsible senior citizen who had been out of work and became quite familiar with the act and regulations. So, I asked him: I will give you Bill C-27 and I would like you to tell me what you think of its content. So he told me: I'll try. I shall
February 1, 1977

read you what he has to say which I feel is worth reading. I quote:
The person who shares his impressions here is a man of some years, with average schooling-equivalent to fourth year high school-who once in his life collected unemployment insurance benefits and to whom was handed the statute book on unemployment insurance in Canada, 1976 edition, as well as a copy of Bill C-27, as passed on first reading concerning unemployment insurance.
After over twenty hours of arduous reading, one reaches the conclusion that those documents are so ambiguous as to represent aberrations on initial reading, which aberrations then go beyond the limits of logic.
One gets the feeling that an attempt is being made at assembling a puzzle that would leave the most able creators in the field-some of whom are famous- flabbergasted and speechless with astonishment.
It seems someone was intent upon creating a maze the like of which schizoph-renes or paranoiacs alone have the secret, or so it seems to me. I have had the same feeling before on hearing music composed solely of perfectly rhythmic discords. I take my hat off to those creators who deserve palms come from the most remote of equitorial jungles.
That gives you an idea of the reaction of one fellow who read Bill C-27 and the act of 1976.
Yet, I am no more stupid that the average guy. Until now, 1 thought I was of average intelligence. But now, I must confess that I suffer from serious complexes for, to my great shame, I must admit I learned very little except that some people can get unemployment insurance according to hypothetical conditions lost in a maze of nebulous considerations reaching from the stratosphere to the depths of Jules Verne's earth.
Yet, I must gather my wits about me and find out who can get, and how, those benefits that seem to come from another planet. Which benefits are measured by a yard stick that has nothing to do with British measures and even less with the metric system.
Now, the dismissed worker will be able to draw UI benefits if he manages to create opportunities for employment through his non initiative by convincing the employers that they will need him in the near future. The pregnant woman will only draw benefits if she has already been on unemployment insurance; if not, implicitly she will have to resort to abortion, secretly of course, be dismissed by her employer, pretend that she is unemployed and draw benefit-I can prove this-and get pregnant again.
This is the only way I know to become entitled to maternity benefits. This is right, is it not? Once again, implicitly; I did read between the lines. If I bore someone a grudge for something unforgivable, to be utterly sadistic, I would implacably condemn him to read these documents and to give a coherent report on unemployment insurance in Canada. But whether or not he succeeds in the long run, he would have the merits that only saints can deserve. Mind you, this man has drawn conclusions from the text of the Unemployment Insurance Act and from the contents of Bill C-27. I have plenty of examples in hand. I will cite a few, I have lots of time. We can say what we think about that legislation. It seems to me that we have got the time today, and there are many workers wishing to take part in this debate, I am sure. I hope there will be as many speakers as possible and that practical suggestions will be made to the minister so that he may improve that piece of legislation. I was told that the premises of the question I raised yesterday were rejected. If you want an idea of how it is working over there, hear what I have to say. Last summer the
Employment and Immigration
construction workers were on strike. Apparently 15,000 workers were affected. I am not a striker, I am a unionist, and I am glad to say it, but I am not a striker.
I find it unfortunate that a large number of unemployed workers underwent some hardship as a result of a strike. However, what is even more unfortunate is that the commission officials took so long before making their investigation. After that, I do not know how they worked. As far as I am concerned, there are some people who dragged their feet in that investigation, since the results took a long time before appearing. I have evidence of it here. Here is an individual who applied for benefits and was told the following: After considering your claim-he had submitted his claim on November 18, and he gets his reply on January 14 and is told: After investigation you were not party to the collective conflict, so you are entitled to benefits. But it took a month and a half to settle that. During that time the unemployed was not getting anything and he had no income. After that try and make me believe that the Unemployment Insurance Commission officials are doing their work properly. They certainly do not work rapidly. You have very clear evidence of that here.
Here we have another worker faced with technical difficulties. It is generally believed that computers costing thousands of dollars and installed in the offices of the Unemployment Insurance Commission should improve the situation. I heard it said once that in some cases people could be paid within two days. It was even suggested on the very same day. It was even suggested that a guy could get a cheque within four hours, a manual payment if it were in particular circumstances. I have personally never seen any. If the minister knows people who were paid within four hours or two days I would be quite happy to know their names because I would be pleased to meet them. Generally it takes a month to five weeks. Why so much with big machines that cost millions and hundreds of public servants who serve or do not serve. So does it take a month, a month and a half to pay an unemployed who needs his money?
Here is another case. The commission tells the guy who submitted his application: We took action on December 16 to allow the processing of weekly reports as of November 21 but we are unfortunately encountering technical difficulties in the settlement of your case. The transactions sent to our regional computer service were returned to us on January 13. So we are taking other means to accelerate the payment of benefits due for the weeks beginning December 5 and 12. We are following this case. That was on January 17. They had technical difficulties.
There are other examples. Another chap from Saint-Gabriel-de-Kamouraska was a construction worker and became involved in the famous inquiry. I point out to the minister that he should pay closer attention to my comments this evening because what I say relates to hardships encountered by workers in my area. There will be less of a surprise for him if he will pay attention and undertake to introduce amendments to help people in need. Indeed, the minister may be in for some surprises as was the case with some of his Quebec colleagues who failed for too long to cater to the poor

February 1, 1977
Employment and Immigration
in their province. It would be better for him to pay close attention. It is a casual advice that I give him.
On August 16, the Commission said: "We received your claim for benefits. In the statement of employment received in September from Aluminium Bridge it says that the work stoppage may be due to a labour conflict; this is not sure, but it could be so. Then, as soon as the decision is known, we will follow-up, and that is all. We are sorry but such is the law." They are always sorry, but it remains that the man gets no benefits. There is another case where due to a complex wording, this inadequate legislation requires the officials to find something to tell the claimants. They have to check the third paragraph of the disqualification notice to the claimant. The legislation and the rules governing the unemployment commission are so complicated that employees, civil servants and others have to resort to incomprehensible phraseology. For those who are listening, try and make something out of this language. Civil servants say to the unemployed: You did not find that if you had not been unable to work as you state, you would have been available to work indeed? This is the text of a letter from the commission. Do you understand anything in that? What do you think a claimant can make out of that?
Here is the case of another worker in the construction industry. The head of special information at the central office in Montreal, 1441 Saint-Urbain Street, mentions in a letter dated November 24 that the renewed application by Mr. Bourgoin has been granted from September 12, 1976 and that steps will be taken on November 24 to expedite the payment of benefits. On the other hand, from the office in Riviere-du-Loup, on December 6 I am informed that payments are stopped after four completed weeks, four consecutive weeks. In the new measure, this has been changed, fortunately! But it took two years of hard work on the part of the commission officials and ministers-two of them-to finally be convinced that there is in the law a provision that prevents people from working. That's true, if they went to work for four weeks in a row during a period when they were unemployed, then they were absolutely disqualified.
More than 100 workers at the Bombardier plant in Sainte-Anne-de-la-Pocatiere were called back two years ago, when Bombardier renovated its Moto-Ski plant, people who were unemployed because the plant was half closed. The company had called back more than 100 workers to work in the plant, so all those people who worked for four or five weeks completely lost their benefits. They were told their claim year was ended. Imagine! It took two ministers and their officials two years and a half to grasp that. Now it is changed. I owe congratulations to those who made that change, it does not happen often that we have the opportunity to congratulate them, so you can applaud them, gentlemen. I would like to applaud everything they do, but there are so many things in there which have to be changed.
I have here another case of job searching, and the difficulty to find a job. It is about a man whose leg was amputated at the knee. I know him well, he is a friend of mine. He even mananged to drive a tractor during 29 weeks. The commission

starts annoying him concerning a visit to an independent doctor. He must go see an independent doctor to check if his leg was really amputated there. Imagine! We see stupid things like that every week. It is really stunning and absolutely ridiculous!
Another one had worked at the Desjardins plant until he had reached age 67. Naturally, he had not applied for Unemployment Insurance benefits; he had been receiving his Old Age Security Pension cheques since he had reached age 65. When he stopped working, he applied for his benefits. This occurred before the implementation of the provisions excluding people 65 years of age. These benefits were paid to him for a few weeks. Then, one day, he was asked to call at the Unemployment Insurance Commission office and offered various jobs. He was even invited to go and work in the Port Cartier as well as Bay James areas. This was a 67 year old man with only one finger in his left hand. How could the Unemployment Insurance Commission civil servants do this to him! They were relying on an Act which does not make sense, which requires complete reviewing and thorough amending.
Suddenly, they realized that they had made a mistake-they come up often enough with wrong figures-and claimed that there was an overpayment of $134 to his credit, as they had disqualified him for refusing to accept employment in the Bay James area. They had disqualified him and paid him $134 in excess. Later, they asked him to reimburse this amount. So I intervened and discussed the matter with the director who was probably the most understanding man in the world but who was under the obligation to apply the most stupid legislation in the world. So, this man was not yet entitled to his guaranteed income supplement since he had worked during the year. So they told me: He must get income from somewhere, he should be able to pay back those $134 since he does not get any supplement! If you can prove that he is eligible for income supplement, may we drop the case. This was pursuant to Section 175(l)(e)ii. By the way, I would really like to hear from the minister, at the first opportunity, how many unemployed people have received $100, $150 or whatever from the Unemployment Insurance Commission, due to an error and how many have been able to avail themselves of Section 175(l)(e)ii. I would really like to know that. So, I have contacted the Unemployment Insurance Commission, and I have not yet been paid, and then-
