speechtext:
I thank all my colleagues for being so tolerant. I suppose they would like to know how this legislation works. I thank them very much. I will try to be as brief as possible, but I want to mention those cases. The Unemployment Insurance Commission keeps asking this 67
February 1, 1977

year old senior citizen-who is now 68 for $ 134. I felt inclined to pay it myself. Really, I was ashamed to see such a team of civil servants. This case became known as far as Montreal. Some of them even told me that they were considering garni-sheeing the savings he had in his bank account. Of course, I insisted that he get his supplement and he got it. I think that he and his wife each got $1,000 in arrears because his case had been pending for a long time. When the Unemployment Insurance Commission learned that they each got $1,000, they wanted the $134 paid back. They did not take into account the debts he had incurred. He had to pay the rent and still had to reimburs this amount. So, the case is still pending. This is why I am asking who can avail himself of this section?
I was talking a while ago about a friend of mine whose views I had sought about the bill dealing with pregnancy benefits-I know that many women get them as I dealt with many cases- but there are also endless complications in some cases. I have in hand a letter by a lady-who, like many other ladies-is not afraid to raise her children and who had been working for 24 weeks. Two months prior to her confinement, she applied for unemployment benefits. She had phoned me before hand to ask me what the procedure was. I told her that it was quite easy. But then, troubles started. She did not receive 10 week benefits. Between the 30th week and the 50th week prior to her confinement: Can you imagine? How foolish can you be?
I am still in contact with the Commission. I received an answer recently. They tried to convince me that she was not eligible for benefits while I knew she was; in spite of all the intricacies in the act, she should be entitled to benefits, it is a matter of common sense. She could not have drawn benefits between the thirtieth and fiftieth week before delivery since she never claimed them. She worked during the qualifying period, namely 24 weeks; why then would the Commission not pay? There are many similar cases. Mr. Speaker; if the minister wants to check, all he has to do is come with his team of civil servants and I shall show him files in my office; he will see by himself what is going on.
It seems that civil servants have been ordered to reduce the number of registered unemployed by 33 percent and the letter I received from this man gives me some reason to believe this. They say: I do not care whether it is you or another. We have received instructions from somewhere. I have been eight years on the board of referees of the Unemployment Insurance Commission in Quebec City. I was representing labour. From time to time we would meet senior officials of the commission and they would give us specific instructions. Of course it was confidential material but I never saw one in favour of the unemployed. They were always at the advantage of the fund. Only I was a worker representative and I did not fear to raise objections whenever valid reasons called for it.
For some time now I have had many occasions to appear before the board of referees to defend unemployed people in a bad position and I have never seen, or very rarely, unless he is more open than average, a union representative who would accept a dissidence on a doubtful case. Most of the time it is a unanimous decision and when there is unanimity, it is written
Employment and Immigration
in the law and permission must be requested from the chairman of the board to refer the case to an umpire. Imagine a chairman who has made a decision three days or a week earlier and finds himself confronted with a request in the following terms: your decision was not correct, could we have the authorization to refer the case to an umpire? What simpleton dare write such ineptitudes in the Unemployment Insurance Commission Act? It seems that with this new legislation, there will be no further need to ask for an authorization from the chairman of the board of referees. That is fine, for I know many lawyers from the legal assistance clinics who are having problems in that respect. It often happens that the board of referees maintain the decisions: they want to keep in good terms with the official. There is nothing so odd in my opinion, when I come before the board of referees, seeing that all of them are nice people. I do not want to over-criticize them, but sometimes the situation seems so strange. The unemployed I represent are asked: Are you aware of our responsibility? They say: No, not exactly. The board says: We are not officers of the commission. We will look over the legislation, and, your case considered in respect to the act and the regulations. If there is any chance of getting benefits paid to you, we will do it. That is what they say to cheer up the claimant. But decisions are delayed until three or four days. They are not taken right away, because too often the office would be upset if decisions were given immediately to some people I know. I told a chap who was not too shy to ask them by whom they were getting paid.
I have been on a board of referees and I know that they are paid by the UIC. Usually, I work for whoever is paying me. They are trying to make people believe that they are totally independent in spite of the fact that they are being paid by the UIC. The setting up of boards of referees was requested by workers' unions, especially by workers' organizations, to help people who were faced with unfair decisions made by UIC officials. This system has solved some of the problems, but it also has to be improved. Thanks to the amendments contained in this bill, no authorization will be necessary. Cases will go to the board of referees but all this process will take time. There are insurability cases pending since 1974. Even today, I have two phone calls related to cases that are pending, because the income tax people say that the employment is not insurable.
Here is the case of a worker who builds homes. He owns a cab in Saint-Gabriel, Kamouraska, but he did some construction work for five weeks. That job was recognized for insurance purposes. Fifteen days later he worked on another house. The work was the same but that job could not be insured because the man was not there often enough to supervise the present worker. Can one imagine such stupid decisions!
Now let us talk about trying to find a job. I have here a fellow from Riviere-Bleue. The man is quite active and once wrote to me to find out if I was in a position to find him work or make suggestions. At first I suggested he get in touch with the manpower people: he could at least visit them. They seldom find you work but in any event it gave him a chance to talk to them. He went to see them. Later on I suggested he

February 1, 1977
Employment and Immigration
write to the Departments of Labour, both in Quebec and in Ottawa, and to everyone who might be able to find him work. I have that correspondence here. The fellow always got a nice reply, but he was told to get in touch with the local manpower people. He received the following answer: We have received your letter of May 4. But I was the one who sent that letter. I wrote to a manpower centre to see what would be their answer in Mr. Bouchard's case. The letter said: This is to inform you that we are sending your letter to our office in Cabano, 14 Commercial Street, as Mr. Bouchard is registered in that centre... From Riviere-du-Loup, this is not very far. There are labour ministers, all kinds of civil servants, all kinds of officers, but he cannot find a job.
How can this be? The minister is responsible for all this, no one can deny it. How is it that the employees of the commission disqualify people because they cannot find a job during a period when there is no work? Look here, I was told that the premises of my question were not acceptable but I can assure you that this is not a way to apply the law either. Somebody will have to change it.
I have here more examples of people looking for jobs, for example this young girl. I communicated with the manpower centre. She has been looking for jobs in 52 different places and she gives all their names. She is a shorthand typist and received a diploma from the school she attended, last June. She has not found a job yet. Today I am told that she will have to make a new application. The unemployed are penalized because they do not find jobs, because they have not searched long enough. But all this monkey business of our administration is madness and this should be changed, the sooner the better.
Recently I received this letter and the minister must have received the same one; it was written by a union leader who I think represents employees of the Public Service Commission and who asked me to retract my words after I said they did not know their job. That is funny. He sent this letter to the minister, who must have received it, to the leader of the Social Credit Party and to myself and he assures me that his people have exceptional qualities. I recognize that many of them are acceptable. But there are four categories of civil servants performing government functions: those who perform, those who perform slowly, those who don't perform at all, and those who perform in the wrong direction. We must be careful with those categories.
I wrote to him, I am not ashamed to say what I wrote. Here is my letter. He sent me back a copy, but I have extra ones in my files. This is a fellow who was ill, he had been hurt in an accident, he had a broken leg. Indeed he has not recovered yet. He may be fit for work again next month. He is still under medical attention. He was visiting with his father-in-law in Saint-Pamphile, in the constituency of Kamouraska-L'Islet.
He went back to Montreal where he had worked before. He went to see his employers to find out if he could resume working, even at a light job. And of course he applied for UIC illness benefits. He was entitled to it, he had contributed enough. The case is before a high-ranking UIC civil servant in
[Mr. Dionne (Kamouraska).J
Ottawa. I phoned him yesterday morning. So he sends a medical certificate, he sends a cheque. The fellow had received a small amount of insurance, a first cheque is deducted, so he is due $12, and on the other one they send him a cheque. Then he gets a notice: Final payment if work is not resumed. The fellow has a broken leg, this is plainly stated in his medical certificate, but final payment if work is not resumed.
So I wrote them because I was getting fed up to hear all sorts of remarks like that. The guy is going to send me the card which reads: final payment if work not resumed. So what did I tell them that crossed them so much? I thought it was very funny, though. That enabled me to know who was sick. Before that I was not too sure but now I know. He asked me to retract. Does it mean I should say; "maybe I should not have written that because you should not always tell the whole truth".
I told the commission guy the man had problems and had sent in two medical reports. The last one was dated December 10. It is obvious that Mr. Bernier was unable to resume work, he has a broken leg, and had to go back to his doctor. I was surprised to hear that the commission had sent him a cheque, the only one ever paid to him since he made his application. And that cheque, said: final payment if work not resumed. I think there are a lot of sick people on the staff of the Unemployment Insurance Commission who should be under appropriate care. In this case it is easy enough to understand that Mr. Bernier will not be able to resume work for several weeks. He has made the required number of payments, he is entitled to sick benefits. Why should the commission civil servants prove so mean? What they want me to retract are those two words-sick and mean. I think this is very funny. It is mean to deny payments and to make no effort to try to find out whether an applicant is eligible for benefits or not. That is being mean. I have nothing to retract on that. As for being sick, well, yes, there are sick people, perhaps sicker than that man who needed benefits. But they are sick in the head, and that is the trouble. There are all sorts of incurable illnesses.
In concluding, I would not want to take excessive advantage of the fact that my colleagues have allowed me to continue. I would like to make a few suggestions, not directly related to the clauses of the bill-I will have an opportunity to come back to them, as I have gone into them very thoroughly-and I think I am in a position to make practical suggestions, concerning phrasing and the legislation such as it was submitted to us. But tonight I shall limit myself to the following: First, we should rephrase the law and rules to make them more understandable, more social, more human, and change our way of implementing them to protect the unemployed instead of the fund; we should retrain, and that is important, as many civil servants as possible, those who do not work or who do not do their work properly, in an atmosphere of practical comprehension, by rotating lay-offs, so they become aware of unemployment related problems through living experiences. Let us lay them off for a while and we shall see their reactions. When they have waited one month, maybe two or three, to get their first benefits, they will be in a better position when they are
February 1, 1977

back on the job to listen to what the unemployed have to say. Maybe they would be eligible for holidays allowances or a severance pay and those moneys will be considered as revenue pursuant to rules 172 and 173.
They would learn to live for a few months under the same conditions as the unemployed and in many cases they could advantageously be replaced by qualified unemployed whose applications for jobs have been on file in the manpower office for months. That would not increase the number of unemployed and would contribute to train a team of civil servants who would be qualified to administer the law and rules, and appreciate the hardships and worries associated with a period of unemployment such as the one we are experiencing now.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-27, which we are debating this evening, is part of the package which the government calls its new employment strategy, and we ought to examine the bill in that context.
If we are to endorse and support a policy for employment, that policy surely ought to meet two basic and vital tests. First, such policy must give individual Canadians the opportunity, encouragement and assistance required to obtain self-respect, adequate income, and satisfying employment. Second, it must do everything in its power to ensure that the priceless human resources of this nation do not go to waste or lie idle; it must ensure the well-being of all people, and see to it that the productivity of all our people is used to its best advantage.
A major contradiction is involved here, Mr. Speaker, because at the very time we are considering this "new employment strategy" which the government has brought forward we are observing in this country, as my colleague mentioned, a monumental increase in the number of unemployed. At present more than 750,000 Canadians are unemployed. They are people who are prevented from contributing productively to our economy.
To this group of unemployed one can add other groups of people who are all too often forgotten and excluded from productive employment. I think, for instance, of young people who are forced to stay in some training program or the classroom because there is no opportunity for them at present to be productively involved in society. I think of the handicapped and the disabled; I think of the elderly who often are forced into idleness although they have many productive years before them. I think of the mothers of young children, mothers who would gladly work part-time, of workers whose jobs make poor use of the skills they have acquired, and of those who are in employment which underutilizes their capacities. Finally, I think of the discouraged worker who has simply dropped out of the labour force because there are no openings for him. Measured in those terms, I believe Bill C-27 is a modest piece of legislation indeed.
I am surprised at the government's attention to this measure, since this bill would open few new vistas for bringing neglected groups or areas into the productive mainstream of
Employment and Immigration
the Canadian economy. Apart from its over-all lack of vision, what disturbs me most about the bill is its insensitive-I might almost say unaware-approach to regional unemployment.
I am somewhat disappointed that the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard) has not yet, to my knowledge, publicly commented on this bill. Unfortunately he is not with us this evening. I certainly hope he will make some remarks at some stage during second reading because much of what I am going to say this evening has a real impact on the portfolio he carries with regard to economic disparities in this country.
I really wonder whether it is accurate to describe this bill as part of an employment strategy. As I said a moment ago, I am particularly concerned and I am going to speak very largely tonight about the implications of this legislation with regard to regional economic and social disparities in Canada. There are aspects of the bill I will not deal with that certainly are open to very real question. I presume other speakers will want to address their attention to them.
There is the question of job training. Over the past few years there has been a series of attempts, with programs under the Department of Manpower, to give people on-the-job training, and opportunities to provide skills and upgrade their education so that they will have better access to and better opportunity on the job market.
After the experience that we have had over almost a decade, it is high time that we know if there is any over-all strategy involved, if there is any realistic co-ordination between the Departments of Regional Economic Expansion, Industry, Trade and Commerce, Transport, or some of the provincial departments which have exercised very active concern and interest in this area. It is not enough to announce we are going to have new pilot projects without giving an evaluation of how effective we have been with previous programs, whether we have learned from them, and how we are going to tailor more clearly job training programs to realistic job needs.
In the area of job-sharing, which the minister commented on briefly this afternoon, there is a great deal of question and uncertainty. My colleague, the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander), gave an indication from his experience of some of the difficulties that have arisen in other countries with regard to this particular proposal.
I am somewhat disturbed by the fact there does not appear to have been much meaningful consultation with either the various provincial departments or agencies that will be responsible in this area, or with the major sectors of the industrial and economic community which obviously will have to take a very activist role.
My present understanding is that organized labour and indeed the industrial community do not look with any great amount of favour or interest upon this proposal. It is somewhat useless for the government to say this is a part of a new employment strategy if in fact there is little interest or cooperation on the horizon from these significant groups.

Employment and Immigration
As I said at the outset, fundamental to any employment strategy must be the recognition that each individual in our society who wishes or requires to enter the labour force should be entitled to do meaningful work at an equitable return. Surely all of us recognize that as an essential requirement. This is essential both for the well-being of individual workers in our society and for the well-being of society as a whole.
When we look at the extent to which people on an individual and collective basis require the help of the whole community, both on an economic and social basis, to say that that must not be the central and beginning point is simply not to recognize the reality itself. As we examine these present changes with respect to the Unemployment Insurance Act, we must look at them against the backdrop of the individual's experience and companion programs which have been in the job creation field. It is a mixed record at best.
We have had programs particularly directed toward young people. Opportunities for Youth comes to mind as a first initiative of the kind of job creation area where people were given sums of money to create, in effect, their own jobs for socially beneficial projects of a short-term nature.
OFY and its companion program, Local Initiatives, which has gone through years one, two, three and four, have given us a great deal of experience with regard to the usefulness, advantages and disadvantages of this kind of job creation experience. In the last month or two the minister has launched the latest addition of these particular kinds of job creation programs with Canada Works and Young Canada Works.
The message is beginning to get through to the minister and some of his officials that all is not well with regard to a continued repetition of a particular, novel approach to job creation. While there have been substantial benefits in terms of some community improvements and some opportunities for people to be engaged in the work force for periods of time, it has not been shown to be at all encompassing or even a major solution with respect to job creation. I hope the minister will be one of the first to recognize this. I do not want to put words in his mouth, but he would not want to be anxious to say that through these programs, whether Local Initiatives or Canada Works, that in itself will affect in a major way the three quarters of a million people presently unemployed.
What disturbs me, and has disturbed me for some considerable time, is that at best these job creation programs are of an ad hoc nature. Their very set-up is an indication of that. Over the past four or five years that these programs have been in operation, there has never been any legislative measure which this parliament, or any of its committees, has had an opportunity to examine with regard to the efficacy of the programs or their required continuation. At best, this is a casual approach to a major expenditure of hundreds of millions of dollars. At worst, it is an indication that the government is not yet ready to say in categorical and long terms what are the benefits of such a program and why it should be enshrined within some form of statute which parliament has had a chance both to scrutinize and give its authority to.

To go on from year to year without any statutory consideration of programs of this nature, which obviously are now becoming somewhat of a permanent fixture, is really to play fast and loose not only with enormous sums of money but with the good will that is in communities, both large and small, from coast to coast in this country. They are willing to accept this form of government intervention, but only if there is proper stewardship connected with it. Unfortunately we have heard enough of abuses that have taken place to realize that public sentiment in a number of areas does not support these job creation programs.
I live in an area where people are so desperate for employment, and have been so concerned as to make the program work satisfactorily, that we have had a very high percentage of commendable projects both for individuals and for communities. However, for us to continue on a year after year basis with the government rushing in from month to month, either creating another kind of ad hoc job creation program or throwing more sums of money into specific regions because the unemployment figures have become absolutely intolerable, is a very irresponsible way for it to provide leadership.
I would hope that this government, even though it may well be in its dying days, would at least try to come to its senses with regard to a more sensible management of this particular initiative. That is all I will say about that particular matter because I know that other speakers will comment on it more extensively.
I want to deal with, as I said at the outset, what I see as a prime problem with regard to Bill C-27. Really it is a form of paradox or strange inconsistency. This is an interesting bill because, as the minister said today, and as was pointed out many months ago by his predecessor during the original budget debate when this proposal was first introduced, there is going to be a raising of the eligibility period from eight to 12 weeks. As my colleague, the hon. member for Hamilton West, reminded the minister again today, this is a policy which we enunciated some years ago and which the government has now, with some very delayed wisdom, accepted. The minister has accepted it and has gone on to estabish another principle about which we have also been equally concerned, and that is to deal with all parts of the country fairly.
Here is where we come to this strange paradox, Mr. Speaker. On page 18 of the bill the minister provides in clause 35 for what will be known as a regionally extended benefit. Then on page 33, and particularly on page 34 of the bill, we discovery what this regionally extended benefit may mean, that there will be in fact extended benefits in areas or regions with unemployment in excess of 4 per cent. Then there are various levels, depending on the percentage of unemployment.
I have no hesitation in saying that I think the government has recognized a fundamental truth about this country, one that it does not recognize very often. Perhaps that is the reason why the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) has just left. I was going to refer to him in particular as one who has had great
February 1, 1977

difficulty recognizing this fundamental truth about Canada. We are not a bland monolith from coast to coast. Perhaps it is not nearly so necessary to say it today with the kind of regional tensions and anxieties which obviously exist in the country, but I believe those who think for a few moments about the varying problems, capacities, concerns and needs of this country will realize that there is a wide variation, not only in regard to such subtle things as attitudes, concepts and understandings, but also in very basic things, such as the ability to work and the wage scales which people receive for similar kinds of employment.
The government is certainly not uninformed in this particular area, Mr. Speaker, because it has been the subject of debate from time to time. The fact that the federal government itself as a national employer has offered various rates of pay for the same kind of work in different parts of the country has been previously questioned. So it is right and proper that with respect to these benefits there is one standard whereby benefits will be based on the number of weeks a person has been employed, which I think form the standpoint of incentive, which concerns all of us very much, is a proper and effective principle to have in place.
Then there is another set of criteria with respect to benefits which relate realistically to unemployment levels in regions across this country. I have not heard anyone, either today or prior to today, when discussing this bill oppose this basic concept of regional variation with respect to benefits. But the part that concerns me is that while the government has accepted, enunciated and established this policy in the legislation before the House today, it has done it for only one side of the equation. The government has said that it should exist with respect to the benefit side, but that it should not exist with respect to eligibility. I am going to say a little more later on about the specific approach which we feel must be taken in order that this piece of legislation be consistent.
As I have said, Mr. Speaker, I am not really giving the government news that it has not been aware of in bits and pieces in other areas of its responsibility. It is just that there is a shocking lack of consistency. In the program of local initiatives to which I referred a few minutes ago it is a well known fact that each year, once the program has been laid out, great attempts are made to judge, on a region by region basis, the exact unemployment situation so that the amount of money available can be tailored to particular needs. In fact in this particular year the variations are so great that the department discovered that certain constituencies could not even make use of their original allotment. Others were receiving two to three times the amount they were originally awarded last September. With respect to the Canada Works Program, as the minister knows, so far as additional provision for capital works is concerned there is no provision for those areas of particularly high unemployment.
We know that one of the fundamental principles of this bill is the bringing together of the Manpower side and the unemployment insurance side in some kind of package, the services being centralized and to a degree made more accessible to the
Employment and Immigration
individual who is looking for employment or to the individual claimant. There may be an additional hidden benefit, apart from the local services factor, or the national planning factor, which the minister has in mind in respect to this new legislation. Perhaps it will allow the department, this new reorganized department, to realize that it must be consistent on its eligibility side as well as on its benefits side. It will, in effect, let one side know what the other side is doing.
In its present context, this particular legislation is what I can only describe, in light of regional realities, as a sort of half pregnant piece of legislation. It is halfway there when it comes to recognizing that there is a particular problem, need or responsibility which the commission has in regard to abnormally high unemployment, and that there must be, as appears from the tables, a specific response to that particular situation.
I suppose that the minister or others might say that the reason we are not providing this eligibility period on a flexible basis is because the situation is basically the same from coast to coast. I think the minister referred to the fact that basically unemployment affects young people, those who are single, or second income earners; and he might also have said it affects those who are women. The implication is given, both in his comments today and in the notes earlier, that there is not really much of a difference whether people are unable to acquire benefits of 12 weeks, whether they live in Summerside, Prince Edward Island, St. John's, Newfoundland, Toronto, Calgary or Vancouver. I want to make it very clear this evening that nothing could be further from the truth.
The minister may now have had a chance to study the figures, but the fact is that the areas that are going to be hardest hit are the very areas with the highest unemployment. It is not surprising, Mr. Speaker, that on a national basis the percentage of those who are going to be affected is something like 13.2 per cent, those who are in the category of eight to 11 weeks entitlement. But when we look at the province of New Brunswick we find the figure there is 18.2 per cent, in Newfoundland it is 17 per cent, in Prince Edward Island it is 15.5 per cent, in Quebec it is 14 per cent, and in Nova Scotia it is 14.8 per cent. In other words, the five eastern provinces with roughly one third the population of Canada will have approximately half their people who have this entitlement from eight to 11 weeks affected.
This means that these provinces are the ones that will bear the heaviest brunt with respect to alternatives-either the alternative of getting some form of employment to increase eligibility to the acceptable level of 12 weeks, or the alternative of drawing social security, or simply the alternative of not generating any income whatsoever. But let there be no mistake that the estimated loss in terms of income on a provincial basis is going to fall extremely heavily, inordinately heavily, on those provinces least able to protect themselves. When we refer to New Brunswick we are talking about $13 million to $16 million. When we talk about Nova Scotia, we are talking about $6 million to $8 million. For Newfoundland the figures are $14 million to $18 million. For Prince Edward Island, something between $2 million to $4 million, and for the

February 1, 1977
Employment and Immigration
province of Quebec, something around S80 million. I know some of the provinces have complained publicly, but I am surprised they have not complained more than they have to date. I suppose this is because they are preoccupied with other things and have not fully realized what a penalty they will be called upon to pay.
I suppose we shall be told that many of these people will find employment of an alternative nature to make up the difference. This is what the minister said in his statement. But look at the job vacancy rate in the Atlantic provinces. It has not exceeded 3,300, yet the statistics show that some 53,000 people in the Atlantic provinces will be directly affected by this change in the provision. If we assume that all of them will be looking for work, this means a ratio of 16 people for each job vacancy that exists.
Even more telling is the impact this measure will have province by province. I think, as I read the figures, we shall see a pattern here which is really serious from the point of view of reinforcing regional economic disparity. As the minister knows, there will be some benefits derived from the suspension of indexing. In 1977 this will mean a total over-all saving of something like $250 million, which will produce a benefit to Newfoundland of something like $4 million, but the loss of income to individual claimants in that province, those who are presently receiving unemployment insurance benefits, will amount to between $24 million and $28 million, leaving a deficit of well over $20 million. With respect to Prince Edward Island there will be a saving of $1 million and a loss of $4 million to $5 million; in Nova Scotia, a saving of $7,750,000 and a loss of $9 million. The province will only lose something like $1,250,000. In New Brunswick there will be a saving of $6 million and a loss of between $19 million and $22 million; in Quebec, a saving of $66,750,000 but a loss of $93 million to $109 million; in Ontario, a saving of $97 million and a loss of between $85 million and $101 million. In other words, Ontario will just be about in balance. In fact, depending on how things work out, there could be some real economic benefit to Ontario. The province of Manitoba will save some $10,500,000 and lose between $7 million and $8 million. Saskatchewan will save $7 million and lose between $8 million and $10 million.
Take a look at the western provinces. In Alberta, they will save some $19,700,000 and lose only between $7 million and $8 million. In British Columbia they will save $29,500,000 and lose in UIC payments between $18 million and $21 million. In the Yukon and the Northwest Territories they will save $1 million and lose between $1 million and $2 million.
These figures are dramatic in their implications when one looks at them in terms of one simple comparison. The Atlantic provinces will be saving $18,750,000 but losing between $56 million and $66 million, as compared with western Canada which will save some $66,500,000 and lose between $40 million and $47 million. It is apparent, therefore, that there is a very real regional impact associated with this bill.

The minister has told us nothing about all this. The information has been given in percentage terms which always reflect an average on a national basis, with an indication that this proposal will affect only certain individuals who are not closely attached to the work force anyway-they are little people who work a few weeks to get enough stamps to draw benefits for a considerable period, and the assumption is that we should not be too concerned about them. The insidious thing about the comments that have been made is this: there seems to have been an attempt to cast aspersions on those who are young, or single, or second-income earners, as though they are somehow a second order of humanity.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext: That is your interpretation.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
It is an interpretation. That is right. And it is one which I make with a very strong assurance. As I studied those figures I realized that a very high proportion of these people are also low income earners, as the minister himself agrees. He told us they have a weaker attachment to the work force. One of the conclusions I draw is that these are the people who are likely to be hit first by any change of program, the people who find it hardest to establish a permanent attachment to the work force. This is not because they are consciously trying to rip-off the unemployment insurance fund but because they are the people who find themselves at the bottom of each and every scale in terms of employability, opportunity, training, and forms of employment available to them. This approach on the part of the government, taking it out on those least able to protect themselves, is not a new approach.
We may have a new minister, but what is being developed here is consistent with what the government has been doing over a considerable period. I would remind hon. members that it was the present government which, only a short time ago, decided to eliminate from benefit possibilities those who are over 65, and decided to reduce benefits for those whose families were larger in size than average. Again a high proportion of such groups live in the very regions which have the highest unemployment rates. On a per capita basis, provinces such as Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick have a much higher proportion of people aged 65 and over than the national average. In those same provinces larger family units are to be found on a per capita basis than in other parts of the country. Yet these are the people who are called upon to bear the effects of these benefit changes.
There is a consistent pattern here. I suppose that as one member coming from a disadvantaged province I should be grateful that the bill at least offers a provision for regional benefits. Maybe the government is taking one timid step toward recognizing that this is a country of regions and that it must respond to the needs of those regions sensitively and reasonably. However, what we have found up to the present is an anti-regional development policy, with the sole exception of the benefit provisions. If the government really wants to harmonize its program with respect to regional disparities- and as the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has often said that
February 1, 1977

this is one of the cornerstones of his leadership-it will need to be more consistent in its legislation than it is in the bill before us.
If there are those who believe that the whole question of opportunity for employment is the same from coast to coast and they have not yet begun to realize that there is some major variation in employment opportunities, I would just like to throw out this one further fact with respect to the seasonality in employment, and I want to make it very clear that one of the underlying problems we face in dealing with abnormally high unemployment in several regions of the country is that far too many of the major industries in these areas are seasonal in nature. We have only to think of industries such as agriculture, fisheries, and tourism to realize the very short duration of employment that is offered in these specific industries.
As one indication of this variation in unemployment rates from the best to the worst month in 1976, let me point out that it was two and a half times greater in terms of variation in Newfoundland than in Ontario, and that was because the province of Newfoundland, perhaps more than any other province in this country, has so much of its industrial employment located around seasonal industries, and until they recognize this, not just in terms of the benefit provisions but also in terms of the eligibility, this legislation represents at best an inconsistent attempt to deal with an employment insurance program for this country.
I said a few minutes ago that the minister referred today- and there have been references previously-to the situation of those who are single, young, or second income earners, but, as I noted, particularly those who are in the low income brackets are in that situation because they are employed in jobs which pay very little and, in far too many instances, provide employment for a short-term period. I am specifically and consciously aware of this fact because during the past few months one of the major industries in my end of Prince Edward Island, that of Irish moss harvesting, has been particularly hard hit. In a good year there may be employment in harvesting Irish moss for perhaps 10 or 11 weeks, of maybe even 12 weeks. In a bad year they will be lucky to get eight weeks. That has certainly been the situation this year. But perhaps I am not telling the government something it does not know because, as a matter of fact, just a few days ago the federal Minister of Fisheries (Mr. LeBlanc) announced a subsidy program because of the particular hardship borne by these Fishermen in PEI and other provinces as well.
I want to come to the essence of what I think is important to make this bill equitable and consistent, and I draw the attention of the minister and of all hon. members to the amendment which my colleague, the hon. member for Hamilton West, indicated today he intends to propose in committee. I think that this is a basic approach, and while affirming our desire to see the Unemployment Insurance Commission move closer to its original insurance principles, he has recognized that it must not be done by attacking the poor, and that any solution must
Employment and Immigration
be highly sensitive to the differences and the composition of our regional work forces.
The amendment would accept the basic 12 week entrance minimum but would allow, in regions of chronic unemployment or seasonal unemployment, the lowering of the minimum down to eight weeks where there would otherwise be undue hardship caused for those who live in those situations. I think this is a fair amendment. Without going into detail, it is certainly consistent with the other parts of this bill where we see, for instance, that regional unemployment rates are used as part three of the benefit structures. I would hope therefore that the minister would seriously consider it when this bill reaches the committee stage. Certainly it fits very clearly with the report of the Economic Council of Canada in 1976 when, in commenting on the general question, in this document entitled "People and Jobs" it states the following, on page 39:
It would, of course, be possible to try to eliminate abuses by cutting certain categories of claimants or the duration of benefits, or by extending the period of work before claimants become eligible for benefits. But such recommendations could prove harmful to persons most exposed to periodic and genuinely and involuntary unemployment. It would seem better to go after "malingerers" more directly. For this reason we believe that much of the problem of abuse of unemployment insurance could be solved by two methods-by tightening administrative efforts to get persons back to work, and by creating jobs to absorb them.
I believe my colleague, the hon. member for Hamilton West, has focused on the problem in the right context. He used the words this afternoon of a new federalism, one that will be realistic and flexible but one which would consistently recognize the basic employment and insurance needs of people in the various regions of this country. I hope that members on all sides of the House, and in particular other colleagues of mine from the Atlantic provinces in other parties, and those who are concerned that we have in effect a national program which adequately reflects the situation in this country, will give favourable consideration to this proposal when it reaches committee and make this in some measure at least a more responsible bill for the Canadian people generally.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe that the main purpose of this bill is to camouflage another major policy shift in the direction and the thrust of the Department of Manpower and Immigration, and one which I predict will be as unsuccessful in meeting the needs of the Canadian people as the earlier reorganizations which have taken place in the last dozen years have been.
I remind the minister that until 1966 we had a national employment service whose function was to find jobs for people who were unemployed, and an Unemployment Insurance Commission whose job was to provide insurance for those who were temporarily unemployed. Then the so-called experts inside the department, and some of the myriad experts from outside who were hired on contract at fat prices, decided that the real trouble in this country, the reason we had so much unemployment, was because our work force was under trained. They ignored the fact that in the last 20 years tens of thousands of young people continued through the high schools, young people who in earlier generations would have left school after

February 1, 1977
Employment and Immigration
grades six, seven or eight. But the panacea for unemployment was to give people training to fit them for the jobs which were supposedly available. So we concentrated on job training.
We built community colleges and technical vocational schools, we spent tens of millions of dollars, we hired teachers and we offered courses. In the estimates for the last fiscal year we provided for job training and training allowances to keep people while they were taking courses $771 million, and in the supplementary estimates, low and behold, there was another $100 million. So we spent $880 million on job training in the last year. With what results? Let me quote from a study done by Barbara Goldman who worked for the C. D. Howe Research Institute, in which she said:
Canada gets a real pay-off from training only if the trainees can find steady employment. Otherwise, training is simply another form of income support, and there are, in many cases, more effective ways of providing income support.
In the same study she pointed out that current manpower programs are heavily weighted toward training, even though the training given does not often match labour market requirements. She pointed out that the amount of manpower training money was often decided not by the needs of the people who supposedly would get the training but by the political considerations of the government. She gave examples. She pointed out that in June, 1975, the then minister announced a $450 million direct employment program to last two years. When he did that the unemployment rate was 7.1 per cent. However, in December of the same year, when unemployment was up to 7.3 per cent, the then president of the treasury board announced cuts in Manpower programs of over $100 million, not because we did not need the money, not because there were not people who needed the training, but simply because it suited the political objectives of the government at that time.
Despite the $880 million we spent on manpower training last year, we have the highest unemployment this country has seen since before World War II. Now the experts are going to break up the existing structure of Canada Manpower centres and the department on the one hand and the Unemployment Insurance Commission on the other, and they are going to amalgamate the two departments into a commission headed by one deputy minister and an assistant deputy minister. I have a great deal of respect for the capacity of these two gentlemen, but they will be responsible for twice as much work as they have been responsible for up until now. I suggest that what we will have is a bureaucratic structure which will collapse under its own weight. However, there is another reason why this program will not work, and that is that the government has no commitment or belief in full employment.
We have heard two members from the official opposition today, and they really believe that many of the people drawing unemployment insurance benefits could in fact be working if only they wanted to. It is obvious the official opposition believes that, because it was the official opposition which first proposed that the period during which people should work before they can draw benefits should be increased from eight weeks to twelve weeks. They reason that many people get a job

and work for eight weeks, just long enough to qualify for benefits. Then they quit and live happily, easily, and comfortably on unemployment insurance benefits. There is just no truth in that kind of thinking.

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-REASON FOR DENIAL OF EXISTENCE OF BLACKLIST OF EMPLOYEES
PUBLIC SERVICE-REASON FOR DENIAL OF EXISTENCE OF BLACKLIST OF EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to return to what I thought was a fairly straightforward question which I asked the Solicitor General (Mr. Fox) last Friday about denials by a top civil servant of the very existence of the now widely known and widely discredited so-called EPO list.
On September 30 of last year, Michael Pitfield, Clerk of the Privy Council, said in a letter to Walter Rudnicki, one of those on the list, the following: "I have never before heard of the concept of an extra parliamentary opposition, least of all one so officially dubbed". He then went on to elaborate.
What I would like to know is how it is that someone in such a high position did not know about this odious list and the silly letter accompanying it, particularly since last October 2 hon. members of this place made inquiries, and while no one knew anything then either, at least notice was, in effect, given.
Months later, confronted by a copy of the list and the letter, however, suddenly official minds and attitudes changed, and the whole matter is really quite shocking. It involves more than just the credibility of this government or a top civil servant. It reminds us of the so-called October crisis which was magnified by this government out of all proportion and became one of the worst blots on the civil liberties of Canadians one could possibly imagine. It also recalls the famous Aislin cartoon of a then prominent cabinet minister carrying Bell Telephone directories in his arms with the caption: "Now we have the list of suspects". All of a sudden lists are in the news again, not separatism this time, but EPO sympathisers, of all things.
The stonewall techniques and the silly, evasive non-answers are just as distasteful in some ways as the list itself. Are we so weak a democracy that we must have lists of young people and students who are radicals of the left or of the right? Are we to be lumped in with the iron curtain countries and former Nazi regimes which epitomize the police state concept, which deal in lists, which dealt in lists of all sorts, and which tolerate no dissenters?
Adjournment Debate
I wonder, when the government House leader was attempting today to avoid the questions of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) by saying that the Pearson guidelines for giving persons singled out for certain purposes a chance to be informed and to defend themselves did not apply in the case of the EPO list, was he thinking how keen he was when minister of immigration to have Mr. Loney dismissed from his summer job and then, before he was even mentioned in the letter-before the list ever compiled-were we in 1971 and are we now so fragile a democracy that we resort to putting young people on lists-in many cases the best and brightest of our young people-merely for having strong views and speaking out, or for being activists.
As nearly as I can ascertain, the "radicalizing of the under classes of society", one of the things that the then solicitor general indicated some of these people on the list were doing, appeared to consist of trying to get a better deal for non-status Indians and Metis people by encouraging them in self-help.
I hope the present Solicitor General will take a strong stand against this sort of listing process and join with us at this time in roundly condemning the whole circumstances and practice. It reminds one of the Christmas rhyme which goes as follows:
He's making a list,
He's checking it twice;
He's going to find out Who's naughty or nice.
In the particular case of the former solicitor general, he personally hand delivered it, and apparently all those to whom he gave it forgot about the whole thing. I have a feeling that Walter Rudnicki and some of the other score of persons will want more justification for what was done than this.
There is a lot of injustice still around, Mr. Speaker. Recently the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) made some comments on the way the Japanese were treated during the war. Perhaps people like Walter Rudnicki, formerly a member of the Public Service of Canada, and Don McCleery and Gilles Brunet and Joe Primeau and others formerly in the RCMP ought to merit some redress and apology while their cases are still current.
In the meantime a little more frankness, openness and information would help a lot, and we will be counting on the Solicitor General for his co-operation in this respect.

Mr. Speaker, in taking part in this debate tonight, I am of course aware that I have only a few minutes to reply to the question asked by the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay). Late on the morning of January 28 last, the hon. member asked me if I knew that certain high officials not under my jurisdiction had supposedly denied at a certain time the existence of the letter read in the House by one of the colleagues of the hon. member, the member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle).
Mr. Speaker, it is not surprising that I was not aware of the letter which had supposedly been written by the Clerk of the

February 1, 1977
Adjournment Debate
Privy Council since I do not usually-I think that we do not usually do this on this side of the House-read the personal mail of other people. In any case, I think that the reply given at that time in the letter to which the hon. member for Central Nova has just referred clearly shows that among both politi-cans in the House and high officials, there never was in their opinion a black list like the hon. member tried to imply in this House.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that it is indeed because this document has constantly been referred to as a black list that it has been mentioned only in general terms without any precision as to the date, so as to make allegations that there may have been a misunderstanding on the subject raised in fact by the hon. member for Central Nova. It is therefore not surprizing that no one on either side of the House ever heard of a black list because, as a matter of fact, there was no such list.
We all know that that the sole responsibility as concerns security that befalls the Royal Canadian Mounted Police consists in gathering information which is then transmitted to the departments and that it is then up to the departments, if they believe the information to be based on fact, after their own evaluation of this information, to apply their own rules. Of course, as the House leader and Acting Prime Minister explained this afternoon, if ever there was any doubt as to the loyalty of the person involved which could lead to a new classification or even to a demotion, a transfer or a simple dismissal, it would then rest with the department concerned to approach the individual, to acquaint him with the doubts raised and thus solve the entire matter.
Mr. Speaker, I think that one of the basic questions raised by the hon. member is the existence of a security service within a state. Nevertheless, when the report of the Royal Commission on Security was tabled in the House in 1969, it was clearly accepted by all the parties in this House that a security service was indeed essential in any democratic country if it did not want to behave like an ostrich in the face of the possible existence of subversive groups.

subtopic: HEALTH-ARSENIC POLLUTION IN YELLOWKNIFE- ACCEPTABILITY OF MEMBERS OF TASK FORCE
HEALTH-ARSENIC POLLUTION IN YELLOWKNIFE- ACCEPTABILITY OF MEMBERS OF TASK FORCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the topic with which I wish to deal this evening concerns the establishment by the Department of National Health and Welfare of a task force to study arsenic pollution in Yellowknife, in the Northwest Territories.
The issue of arsenic pollution in Yellowknife is not new, by any means, since Yellowknife residents have known about arsenic pollution for some years. On January 18 of this year, as the arsenic story broke in the newspapers, an early Yellowknife pioneer by the name of Charles H. Schwerdt wrote me a long letter in which he described Yellowknife in the 1930's and 1940's. Mr. Schwerdt is retired and presently living in Surrey, B.C. He stated that residents of Yellowknife were aware of arsenic pollution even in those days. I shall quote part of the letter he wrote. He said:
We had arsenic pollution of snow, water, vegetation all over the area as early as the spring of 1947-exactly some 30 years ago.
I do not know if any records are in existence at this time to establish certain facts...
This I do know. One Mr. Callaghan, known as the Peace River farmer, brought some milk cows and other stock in Yellowknife, hoping to establish a dairy farm there. I believe that was in the summer of 1944 or 1945, but not certain. However, this I do know. He lost all of his stock in less than a year after bringing them. Dr. Stanton, who was the resident doctor at the 'Con' mine, diagnosed and established the cattle died from arsenic poisoning on the vegetation. Plus the water. What compensation he was given I do not know.
That was the situation around 1947, Mr. Speaker. Over the years there have been many studies on arsenic, and people are losing confidence in the government's ability to cope with the problem; but the minister has announced yet another study, which I welcome, although with reservations. One of my reservations is that so many such studies have been undertaken over the years.
The Grainge report, which is part of the Yellowknife environmental survey, lists 24 separate studies on environmental conditions in Yellowknife in the last ten years alone. Most of those studies dealt with arsenic pollution. One study done in 1969 neglected to inform the public about such dangers as unsafe drinking water in Yellowknife Bay. The YES study indicated that there is a high level of arsenic in the snow. These and other examples over the years show that residents of Yellowknife have reason to be suspicious of the federal health department.
I also have reservations about the terms of reference of this task force, as set out in the minister's news release of January 18, 1977. There is no indication that this task force intends to break new ground. It is instructed to review all available data relevant to arsenic in the Yellowknife area; and, 24 official studies having been done in the last ten years alone, I wish them luck. But the minister has not laid down instructions for the testing of specific groups, particularly miners and people living in the Indian villages near Yellowknife.
On January 15, at a press conference I attended in Toronto, the National Indian Brotherhood and the United Steelworkers issued a statement declaring that there is a most serious arsenic problem in the Yellowknife area. As a result of these charges and the national publicity in the media, the minister announced the establishment of the task force.
One fact which came across clearly in the NIB and Steelworkers press release was that certain specific groups in the Yellowknife area, especially miners and certain Indian people, have come into contact with high levels of arsenic. However, little provision has been made in the terms of reference of the task force for directing the task force to examine closely these specific groups. Perhaps the general health of Yellowknife residents is good, and the exposure to arsenic low; but if certain groups are being exposed to unacceptably high, even dangerous levels of arsenic, the federal health department ought to act quickly.
I call for immediate action with respect to the Indian children tested by the National Indian Brotherhood. I also call on the task force to examine closely the working conditions of

February 1, 1977

those working in the mill and the mines. We know that the arsenic in the area is the result of the mining operations in that region. Mr. Speaker, the people of the region must risk exposure to arsenic on a daily basis in order to provide a home for their families. Surely, since the task force is to deal with arsenic and the dangers it creates to one's health, the first priority should be to examine workers who are in daily contact with it.
I would also point out to the minister that I found out earlier today that both the National Brotherhood and the United Steelworkers of America are highly dissatisfied with two of the three members on the task force, namely, Dr. Mackenzie and Mr. Tupper.
These two groups have asked, right from the day the minister announced the task force, that the members of this body be acceptable to all parties concerned, the mining companies, the unions, the Indian bands, and the federal health department. It was to this matter that I referred when I questioned the minister on January 24 of this year. As a result of appointment to this task force many concerned groups are prepared to be cynical of any findings even before this task force has had its first meeting.
The residents of Yellowknife are proud of their community. They are not ashamed of hard work, and they have adapted to a cold and often harsh environment in the northern half of our nation. Because they do work so hard they have the right, I repeat the right, Mr. Speaker, to expect the government to act responsibly in protecting their health and environment.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-REQUEST FOR RECONSTITUTION OF COMMITTEE ON INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-REQUEST FOR RECONSTITUTION OF COMMITTEE ON INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week I concluded a speaking tour of 16 Canadian cities where I discussed with audiences across the country the subject of Canada and the Third World future. This journey followed a six-week study tour of development in Asia, where I visited China and also examined the operation of the Canadian International Development Agency (CIDA) in Indonesia and Bangladesh.
Thus in the past few weeks I have been able to examine Canada's foreign aid in the field itself, and also to observe the reaction of Canadians across the country to CIDA's $1 billion program. I made a similar tour of Canada one year ago and found widespread confusion about the effectiveness of aid.
I am sorry to report that confusion has worsened in the past year. There is now, in fact, a crisis of confidence in CIDA. The agency has been attacked for "goofs", the Auditor General of Canada has criticized "a serious internal control weakness," and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has let the agency drift without full-time ministerial leadership. Canadians are now asking where CIDA is going. Until that question can be adequately answered by the government, CIDA will continue to suffer from an appalling image across Canada.
I found Canadians generally to be in favour of assisting developing countries, and I want to underline that fact. There is still support for Canada's involvement in helping developing countries, but the declining credibility of CIDA is undermining that very support for foreign aid. That is the point I want to bring home to the government tonight in asking that there be an overhaul of CIDA. This overhaul is now imperative to restore the support of parliament and the public in the strengthening of Canada's relations with developing countries.
The sub-committee on international development which received a reference from the House just prior to Christmas will begin its hearings this month. I think those hearings must attempt to get beyond the superficial criticisms of CIDA which we have been hearing from such critics as Dr. Morton Shulman, who has been raising questions which, whatever validity there may be to the charges raised, are still peripheral questions and do not address themselves to the heart of the question. The heart of the question is: does Canadian aid actually help the people for whom it is intended, and is it getting through to them?
I found on my tour of Asian countries, particularly Indonesia and Bangladesh, which are among the top ten aid recipients of the Canadian government, that not enough of our aid is getting through to the village level and that there ought to be greater emphasis on the community level. I think more attention should be paid to those projects that reach people's

February 1, 1977
Adjournment Debate
lives and which enable them to take hold of development in their own lives. This would entail at the very least the raising of the priority of funding available to non-governmental organizations within the existing CIDA budget so that there would be a greater ability on their part to take part in community development in Asia.
So, Mr. Speaker, I am making an appeal for an improvement in the quality of CIDA's aid as distinct from increasing the quantity. The question of quantity is now, to my mind, a secondary question. The first question is to improve the quality. In order to do this certain steps must be taken. It is now obvious that the external affairs minister has neither time nor the inclination to control CIDA as it must be controlled. Here is a $1 billion agency that is not receiving any sort of full time ministerial control. The agency does need its own minister to control its far flung operations and to report on them to parliament. There is too much money involved for it to be given casual ministerial supervision.
This question has been floating around Ottawa for the past several months. It is time that the Prime Minister took specific action and made that change in CIDA's leadership. I think it is time now to re-evaluate our aid to Cuba and to consider cutting off aid to that country. Whatever good CIDA's agricultural projects are doing in Cuba, it is not possible to support them when Cuba finds the resources to send troops to Angola, and also now to train guerrillas for war against Rhodesia's white minority. The expulsion of Cuban diplomats from Canada for conducting an intelligence operation in Montreal raises further questions about CIDA being duped.
In other words, I think every so often CIDA must re-evaluate the actions of countries that are receiving our aid, and if indeed they do have resources to conduct spurious activities I think it is a solid enough reason to reconsider aid. The parliamentary sub-committee on international development must deal with the basic question I raise of whether aid is getting through to the village level, and of an increase in priorities.
Finally, CIDA ought to start a concerted drive of development education in Canada so that Canadians would have a better understanding of the actual help that CIDA is providing, along with the limitations of aid. There are many good things about CIDA. It is not only a question of the mistakes made by the agency. Canadians, as well as the members of this House, need to be able to get a balanced appraisal in order to have a proper judgment made of the value of this very important agency. The CIDA five-year strategy for international development co-operation has been in existence now for 18 months and supports the trade and monetary changes called for by the United Nations. I am sorry to tell the House that Canadians hardly even know of the existence of that strategy, and for that I blame the government for putting its own strategy on the shelf.
I think the time has come when those who feel warmest toward the aspirations of the Third World should probe the faults and failures of policies in both the developed and developing nations. Only such a thorough probe which the

committee would be able to give if it had access to complete information about CIDA, including country reports, will help Canadians have a deeper appreciation of our changing role in developing nations. Only that kind of study will help us go beyond aid so that we can take part in the structural changes called for by the United Nations, and bring the Canadian public along with us.
